docs.title: IncubaCloud Documentation
docs.text:
IncubaCloud is a PaaS for Odoo: it gives you a control plane to deploy, operate and bill multi-tenant Odoo instances on your own infrastructure or on hosted VPS — with single sign-on, automatic backups, custom domains, and zero glue code on your side.

This site documents the platform from a user's perspective. Quickstarts live on the marketing site's /docs section; the rest — every screen, every option, every troubleshooting note — lives here.

One product, two ways to run it

IncubaCloud is a set of Odoo modules you install on your own Odoo 19.0: the code is on GitHub, free to install and use, and INSTALL.md says what it needs. The same panel also runs as a hosted SaaS (incubacloud.io: signup, plans, on-demand VPS, managed backup storage). The control plane you use day-to-day is the same in both. Pages and sections that only exist on the hosted service are marked with an IncubaCloud SaaS admonition like this one.

docs.title: Need help?
docs.text: The fastest way to reach us is through the contact form. For bug reports and feature requests, open an issue on GitHub.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
An AI agent — Claude Code, Claude, Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, Codex — can work on your panel for you: look at projects and instances, read logs, deploy, back up, clone a staging, change settings. It connects to the panel's MCP address and acts as you: with your role and your projects' access, never more.

With a developer's role, an agent also works on your project's GitHub repository: it reads it, creates branches, commits and opens pull requests; writing to a branch that existed before waits for your approval. The panel has an assistant of its own too, inside the panel: see Assistant.

What an agent does not get:

  • Secrets. Passwords, keys and tokens never reach it, and it cannot set them: you set them in the panel. See Secrets.
  • A free hand with what cannot be undone. Deleting, restoring, moving, trusting a server's key, signing in to an instance, downloading a backup, running a command on production or on a server, and changing security settings wait for your approval. See Approvals.
  • Uploads and interactive terminals. Uploading a backup to restore and the live terminals stay in the panel; agents run one command at a time.

Everything an agent changes is in the audit log under your name, followed by via agent and which one.

docs.title: Auto-approval
docs.text:
Auto-approval lets one credential of one person act without asking, until a date or with no end date: an API key, an OAuth client (an MCP client the person signed in with), or the panel's assistant. While the rule is active, every action that would wait for an approval runs at once. Every other agent keeps asking.

It is for an agent you leave working on its own — a dedicated key for an automation, say — while the agents you use day to day keep asking you first. It is off until an Administrator grants a rule.

What you give up

An approval is the moment a person reads what an agent is about to do. With a rule there is none, for every action the person's role allows, production included. Read the risks below before you grant one.

docs.title: What runs without asking
docs.text:
Everything the Approvals page lists, and nothing is held back: deleting projects, instances, servers and backup destinations; restoring over production; commands on production instances and on servers; security settings and purging the audit log; sign-in links and backup downloads; writing to any branch and to public repositories. For the assistant, also what it would show a card for, including changes after it read logs, files or mail.

What stays as it is: the person's role and projects, every check the panel makes before it would ask (an action it refuses is still refused), secrets (they never reach an agent), and the limits on calls.

IncubaCloud SaaS

Auto-approval is not available yet on the panels of IncubaCloud SaaS: Settings → Agents (MCP) says so, and a grant is refused. Once it is, charges are the exception you choose: the actions that charge money — orders, purchases, plan changes billed to your account — stay out of a rule unless you tick Include charges when you grant it. Without it they keep asking, as before; with it they run without asking too. The notice, the list of rules and the agent's list of tools say whether a rule includes them.

docs.title: The risks
docs.text:
The panel stops protecting you from three things:

  1. The model's mistakes. A wrong call — another instance, another backup — runs at once. Agents treat "the panel asks first" as a safety net and call a tool to propose an action; with a rule there is no net. Deleting, restoring over production, continuous recovery and removing a frozen copy cannot be undone.
  2. Instructions hidden in what the agent reads: a log, a captured mail, a file of a repository, a command's output, the end of a job, an alert, and anything it reads outside the panel, such as an issue or a web page. If the agent follows them, they run, on production too, and nobody sees them before. What such an instruction aims for is deleting or restoring, a command on a server, or taking data out: a sign-in link, a backup download, a public repository, or the notifications sent to another chat.
  3. A leaked credential. Whoever holds the key or the client's token acts as that person, without asking, until the rule ends. Revoke the rule and the credential.

Also keep in mind:

  • A rule for an Administrator reaches everything an Administrator does: security settings, trusting a server's SSH key without anyone comparing it, commands on every server — the panel's own included, from which their agent can write to the panel's database, rules too — and purging the audit log.
  • An agent that drives an Administrator's browser, with the panel open, can grant a rule, as it can approve an action: the panel refuses a grant that comes through an agent's connection, but cannot tell a browser an agent drives from the person.
  • Whoever has a shell on the panel's server, or is Odoo's system administrator, has the panel's database, and with it the rules.
  • With an OAuth client, the rule covers every session of that person with that application, on any device. Disconnecting the agent does not end the rule: if the person connects the same application again, it applies again. Revoke the rule too.
  • Who answers for it. The audit names the person whose credential acted, not the Administrator who granted the rule.
  • Revoking does not undo. What already ran, or is queued, stays.
  • The audit records actions, not reads. It says what the agent did, not what it had read before doing it.
  • The audit is not kept for ever. Its retention (Settings → Logs & retention → Audit log retention), Purge old logs now and an agent's purge_audit_logs delete old rows, those of what a rule approved included; the rule, its count of calls and its last use stay. A rule's Activity may then list fewer actions than it counts.

docs.title: Grant a rule
docs.text:
Only an Administrator grants a rule, from the panel; no agent's connection can grant, extend or revoke one.

  1. Connect the agent first: a rule is granted to a credential that has already connected to the panel (the assistant is offered for the people who use it).
  2. Open Settings → Agents (MCP) and choose Grant auto-approval….
  3. Choose the Person, their Credential (each one shows its id and when it last connected, so two keys with the same name are told apart), and how long: 7, 30 or 90 days, No end date, or until a date. Nothing is chosen for you; the panel recommends 90 days, the usual rotation period of a credential. A rule with no end date lasts until it is revoked, the API key is deleted or the person is archived: how long is your decision, and a date is safer.
  4. Read the notice. It names the person, the credential and the date (or says the rule has no end date) and lists the risks above. Tick I understand, and I take responsibility for what this agent does without asking and choose Grant auto-approval.

The panel keeps who granted it, when, from which address and which version of the notice. A rule cannot be extended: when it ends, grant a new one, with the notice again. Granting a rule to a credential that has one replaces it.

docs.title: When a rule ends
docs.text:
A rule stops approving at once, at the next call, when:

  • its date passes, if it has one;
  • it is revoked: an Administrator revokes any rule, and a person their own, from Settings → Agents (MCP), or from Connect an agent;
  • the person is archived: their rules end, and stay ended if the person is reactivated;
  • the API key is deleted or expires.

When the person's role goes up, the rule is paused: it was granted for what the person could do then. An Administrator grants a new one if it should cover the new role.

docs.title: Where you see it
docs.text:
• Settings → Agents (MCP): every rule, with its person and role, credential, who granted it and when, its date (or No end date), when it was last used, how many calls it approved, and its state (active, paused, expired or revoked). Activity lists what the rule approved, with its grant and its end.
  • Connect an agent: the person a rule covers sees … acts without asking until … (or … with no end date), with Revoke.
  • The audit log of instances and servers: auto-approved after the agent's name (the rule and who granted it, on hover), and approved when the person approved the action.
  • The jobs: the history and an instance's activity show via agent … · auto-approved under the user.
  • The assistant's chat: each action shows ran without asking, and says so when the assistant had read content other people can write.
  • The agent itself: its list of tools says which run without asking, and until when (or that the rule has no end date).

docs.title: Approvals
docs.text:
Some actions wait for you, whatever the agent asks:

  • deleting a project, an instance (archived or not), a server or a backup destination;
  • restoring a backup or continuous recovery, and replacing a staging's data with a copy of production;
  • moving an instance or undoing a move, and resetting the GitHub App;
  • trusting a server's SSH key: you see the key trusted until now and the one the server presents now; compare them before approving;
  • a sign-in link to an instance: you see the instance's user (name, login and id), whether it is an administrator and whether the instance is production;
  • a download link for a backup: you see the file and the instance;
  • writing to a branch of a repository that existed before the agent created it, saying so when a production instance rebuilds from it; anything written to a public repository; a pull request in a public repository, or in a project that makes a preview of production for each pull request; creating a repository and connecting one to a project;
  • a command on a production instance, and every command on a server: you see the exact command;
  • purging the audit log, and changing a security setting — the audit retention, the trusted proxies (the panel's, or a server's), a rate limit (the agents' included), the agents' issuer or the MCP address, and, on IncubaCloud SaaS, the observability settings: you see each value before and after.

An action the panel would refuse anyway — your role does not allow it, the production instance cannot be refreshed — is refused before you are asked.

docs.title: How you are asked
docs.text:
It depends on your client:

Client What you see Clients that show forms A yes/no question inside the client, saying what will happen. Clients that open links The client opens the panel's approval page; once you approve, it goes on. Other clients The agent gives you a link to the panel's approval page; after approving, ask it to try again.

The approval page needs your panel session: sign in as yourself, if you are not. Another user cannot answer it, and you cannot answer theirs. It shows what will happen — a command in a block of its own — with Approve and Cancel. Cancelled, the agent does not do it.

An approval lasts ten minutes and is used once, by the agent that asked: the same action again asks again, different values ask anew, and another of your agents (another client or API key) cannot use it.

What an approval protects you from

It protects you from the agent's mistakes and from instructions hidden in a log or an email that the agent read. It does not protect you from a client you should not trust — such a client can answer "yes" by itself — nor from an agent that drives your browser while your panel is open: it can open the page and approve. Connect only clients you trust, and revoke any you stop trusting.

An Administrator can let one credential of one person act without these approvals, until a date or with no end date: see Auto-approval.

docs.title: Connect an agent
docs.text:
Open the user menu (your name, top right) and choose Connect an agent. The page shows this panel's MCP address, with a button to copy it, and the steps for each client, with the address already in every command.

How your agent signs in depends on the panel:

  • With OAuth (IncubaCloud SaaS, or a self-hosted panel with an OAuth provider for agents): the first time, the agent opens a page where you sign in and allow it, as you do in the browser.
  • With an API key (a self-hosted panel without one): you create a key and the agent sends it with every call. See Self-hosted panel without OAuth.

IncubaCloud SaaS

Your agent signs in with your IncubaCloud account. Your user must exist on the panel: if you were invited and never opened the panel, open it once first.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
Run, with your panel's address:

claude mcp add --transport http --scope user incubacloud 'https://<your panel>/mcp'

Then run /mcp in Claude Code and choose incubacloud to sign in.

docs.title: Claude and Claude Desktop
docs.text:
1. In Claude, open Customize, then Connectors, and choose + Add, then Add custom connector.
  2. Name it, for example IncubaCloud, paste the panel's MCP address and choose Continue.
  3. Keep the sign-in settings Claude detects, choose Continue, then Add, and sign in.

To use it in a conversation, choose + at the bottom left of the chat, then Connectors, and switch it on.

On a Team or Enterprise plan, an Owner or Primary Owner adds the connector once, in Organization settings, Connectors (Add, Custom, Web); then each member finds it in Customize, Connectors, and chooses Connect.

The panel must be reachable from the internet

Claude connects from Anthropic's servers, not from your computer. A self-hosted panel on a private network, behind a VPN or a firewall that blocks them cannot be added this way.

docs.title: Cursor
docs.text:
Choose Add to Cursor on the panel's page, or add this to ~/.cursor/mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "incubacloud": {
      "url": "https://<your panel>/mcp"
    }
  }
}

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text:
Run:

code --add-mcp '{"name":"incubacloud","type":"http","url":"https://<your panel>/mcp"}'

docs.title: Codex
docs.text:
Add this to ~/.codex/config.toml:

[mcp_servers.incubacloud]
url = "https://<your panel>/mcp"

Then run this to sign in:

codex mcp login incubacloud

docs.title: Other clients
docs.text: Add a remote MCP server of type HTTP (streamable HTTP) with the panel's MCP address. The client must support OAuth, or, on a self-hosted panel without OAuth, send an API key in a header.

docs.title: Self-hosted panel without OAuth
docs.text:
Without an OAuth provider for agents, the page says This panel accepts API keys only, and every command it shows carries the key.

  1. Open your preferences (the page links them), tab Security, API Keys, and choose Add API Key.
  2. Odoo asks you to confirm who you are first: your password, or, with two-factor authentication, the code of your authenticator app (or a passkey, where your account has one).
  3. Give the key a Description — the client's name, for instance — and a Duration (the longest Odoo offers depends on your user's groups), then Generate key. Copy it: it is shown once. Treat it like a password; the agent acts with it as you, with your role, until you revoke it.
  4. Use the commands the page shows. Where one says <API_KEY>, put your key; where it names the environment variable INCUBACLOUD_API_KEY, set that variable to your key before you start the client.

Every command the agent then wants to run on a server or on a production instance, and every deletion or restore, waits for your approval, with the exact command shown: see Approvals.

Client How it sends the key Claude Code claude mcp add --transport http --scope user incubacloud 'https://<your panel>/mcp' --header "Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>" Claude and Claude Desktop When adding the connector, in the sign-in settings choose No sign in and, under Request headers, add Authorization with the value Bearer <API_KEY>; then choose Continue and Add. Request headers is in beta in Claude and not every account has it: if you do not see it, use Claude Code or another client. On an individual plan only: a connector an Owner or Primary Owner adds in Organization settings is shared by every member, and so would your key be. Cursor ~/.cursor/mcp.json with "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ${env:INCUBACLOUD_API_KEY}"}: Cursor reads the key from the environment. There is no one-click link: it would carry the key. VS Code code --add-mcp with "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer <API_KEY>"} Codex bearer_token_env_var = "INCUBACLOUD_API_KEY" in config.toml: Codex reads the key from the environment. Other clients The header Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>.

IncubaCloud SaaS

The panels of IncubaCloud SaaS accept OAuth only: an API key is refused, whoever created it.

A server with several databases must select the panel's database by name, with db_name or dbfilter = ^<name>$; without it, /mcp answers 404. A filter by host name (%h, %d) also stops the panel's jobs: INSTALL.md.

The address the page puts in every command is Settings → Agents (MCP) → MCP address; left empty, it is the panel's own address (web.base.url) followed by /mcp. Odoo rewrites web.base.url to the address in the browser each time a user with access to Odoo's Settings signs in, so the default follows whoever signed in last. Set the MCP address to the address your computers reach the panel at, or fix web.base.url with the system parameter web.base.url.freeze set to True. A panel only your network reaches, with Claude Desktop: Panel on an internal network.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
What Limit Calls of all your agents together 120 per minute by default (managers change it in Settings → Rate limits) One answer 20 KB, under the 25,000 tokens Claude Code takes from a tool by default; longer logs, lists and mail come in pages, and the agent asks for the next one; a command's output is cut and says so A command (run_command, run_host_command) 60 seconds; what it leaves running in the background is not stopped. The terminal's rate limits apply An approval 10 minutes, used once A backup download link 15 minutes, used once A sign-in link to an instance 60 seconds, used once An agent's access (IncubaCloud SaaS) Renewed by the client every few minutes while you do not revoke it; cut off after 30 days unused

Long operations — deploy, rebuild, backups, clones, restores, moves — answer at once with a job, which the agent follows until it ends.

docs.title: Revoke an agent
docs.text:
IncubaCloud SaaS

Open Connected agents in your IncubaCloud account (the panel's Connect an agent page links it). It lists each agent with its panel, when you allowed it and when it was last used. Revoke cuts it off: its access ends within five minutes, and it cannot renew it.

Signing out of your IncubaCloud account does not disconnect your agents: they do not depend on your browser's session. An agent unused for 30 days is cut off on its own.

On a self-hosted panel:

  • With API keys, delete the agent's key in your preferences (Security, API Keys): its next call fails.
  • With your own OAuth provider, revoke the agent's grant there; its access ends when its current token expires.

Whatever the agent holds, a user who is deactivated, or who no longer has a role on the panel, is refused at once.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
Passwords, keys and tokens — servers' passwords and SSH keys, databases' passwords, backup destinations' keys, the GitHub App's key, notification tokens — never go to an agent and never come from one.

  • Where the panel shows a secret as set or not set, the agent sees the same: whether it is set, never its value.
  • An agent that tries to set one is refused: Secrets are changed in the panel, naming the argument that carried it. A server an agent adds has no SSH credentials until you set them in the panel; a backup destination needs its key set in the panel.
  • Whatever an agent reads — logs, command output, job logs, alerts, captured mail — has every secret the panel keeps replaced by [secreto], as are a password or a token written into a web address. In captured mail, links that sign someone in or reset a password are replaced too.

A safety net, not a guarantee

An agent allowed to run commands in an instance can read that instance's secrets, exactly as the terminal can, and could change them before showing them. Give that role to agents you trust.

docs.title: Assistant
docs.text:
The assistant is a chat inside your panel. Ask it how the panel works, what an error in your logs means, or to do something for you — deploy, back up, clone a staging, or write a small Odoo module and try it on a staging.

It works as you: with your role and your projects' access, never more. What your role cannot do in the panel, the assistant cannot do either. It is an AI, not a person, and it can make mistakes: check its answers and its changes before you rely on them.

docs.title: Open it
docs.text:
The Assistant button is in the top bar, before your user menu. It is there only if a manager of the panel turned the assistant on and chose you as one of its users (see Settings). It opens the chat on the side, over the page you are on: the assistant knows which project, instance or server you have open.

The first time, a notice — Before you use the assistant — tells you what the assistant sends to the AI provider (see Privacy and limits); press I understand to start. Next to the message field the panel always shows that you are chatting with an AI and where your messages go.

The top of the panel shows what you have spent this month, approximately, and your limit if the panel has one. The Model list in a conversation offers the models a manager allowed.

When a manager turns the assistant off, or takes you out of its users, nothing new can be asked: the button stays while you have conversations, to read or delete them (see below).

docs.title: What it can do
docs.text:
• Answer from the documentation, with links to the pages it used, and from the panel's public code when the documentation is not enough.
  • Look at your panel: projects, instances, jobs, alerts, logs.
  • Diagnose: read a failed job or an instance's logs and explain what went wrong.
  • Operate: deploy, rebuild, back up, clone a staging, change settings — what your role allows. Creating instances, deploying and rebuilding need the developer role.
  • Write Odoo modules in your project's GitHub repository (developers and managers): see below.

Long operations are jobs: the conversation waits for them and goes on when they end (Waiting for a job…). You can close the panel, or the browser: the assistant keeps working, and the button shows a number when conversations have news for you. What you write while it is working waits as queued and is read before its next step. A conversation does one task at a time.

IncubaCloud SaaS

On a plan whose panel sleeps while nobody uses it, a task can stop if the panel falls asleep: open the conversation once it is awake and press Retry.

docs.title: Confirmations
docs.text:
Almost every change waits for you to confirm it in the chat, whatever the assistant asks. The exception is the work of trying something on a staging: deploying, rebuilding or backing up a staging, keeping it, dismissing a single alert, tags, and the code on the assistant's own branch. So, among others, these always wait for you:

  • deleting, restoring, moving, emptying a staging's mailbox, dismissing all alerts, and anything an agent would need your approval for;
  • anything that reaches a production instance, however the assistant names it: the card says This changes production;
  • creating an instance (it takes the server's CPU, memory and disk), and running a command in an instance, a staging too;
  • changing a project's or an instance's repositories or branches (the card lists what is added, removed and moved), creating or connecting a repository;
  • writing to a branch that existed before the assistant created it, to a branch a production instance deploys from (the card names it), or to a public repository; opening a pull request in a public repository, or in a project that makes a preview of production for each pull request;
  • after the assistant read something other people can write — logs, files of your repository, mail a staging caught, a command's output, or a project and its jobs when a member with a lower role than yours can change them — every change, until you write again while the assistant is not working: that text could carry instructions the assistant must not follow. A message you send while it works does not lift this. This includes the work on the assistant's own new branch and redeploying its staging, which otherwise need no card.

The assistant reads only repositories of your projects and instances, and writes only to those of your projects. A branch counts as the assistant's when an agent of yours created it, from any conversation or connected client: writing to it asks for no card, except after the assistant read text others write in that task, until you write again.

The card says what will happen, with Confirm and Cancel. Only you can answer it, from your browser: the assistant cannot confirm its own actions. A card lasts ten minutes, and once confirmed it is used once; writing a new message instead of answering it cancels it, and the assistant is told.

An Administrator can grant your assistant an auto-approval rule, until a date or with no end date: then none of these shows a card, including after the assistant read text others write, and each action says ran without asking in the chat. Read its risks first.

docs.title: Writing a module
docs.text:
Ask for what you need, in your words: "Add an Internal code field to contacts and show it on the contact form". The assistant:

  1. reads your project, its repository and its Odoo version;
  2. creates a new branch, assistant/<what it does> unless you name it;
  3. writes the module there, in one or a few commits;
  4. offers to create a staging that deploys from that branch (a card), and deploys it;
  5. installs the module on the staging with a command in the instance (a card: a deploy installs no module of yours), and updates it after each change;
  6. when something fails, reads the logs, fixes, commits, rebuilds and updates;
  7. when it works, gives you the staging's address and opens a pull request.

Once it has read your repository's files or the staging's logs, each of these steps asks for your card, until you write again (see Confirmations).

Moving it to production is always a separate step that you ask for, and it is confirmed. Your project needs a GitHub repository: without one, the assistant offers to create a private one in your GitHub account (with the panel's personal access token) and to connect it, or explains how to create it yourself.

The panel's GitHub App only reads your code: the panel writes with the personal access token saved in Settings → GitHub. Never under .github/ (workflows run with your repository's secrets), and never a password or a key of the panel in a file. A new branch or a pull request starts whatever workflows your repository already runs on them.

docs.title: Stop, retry, continue
docs.text:
• Stop ends the task at the next step. What was done stays as it is: a commit on the branch, a staging.
  • Retry goes on after an error or a stop (the AI provider did not answer, say).
  • A task stops after a number of steps (30 unless a manager changed it) and asks whether to go on: Go on continues.

docs.title: Your conversations
docs.text: The panel keeps each conversation 30 days after its last activity, and only you can read them in the panel — not a manager either. New conversation opens another; the trash icon deletes one (press Delete it to confirm), at any time, also while the assistant is off for you. What the assistant does is in the audit log under your name, via agent Assistant (conversation N).

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text: What you see What to do The AI provider refused the panel's key. A manager changes it in Settings → Assistant. The AI provider's account has no credit left. A manager checks the account on the provider's site. The AI provider is busy. / is not answering. Retry in a moment. The panel could not reach the AI provider. The server cannot open the provider's address: a manager checks the server's access to the internet. You reached your monthly limit. It goes on next month, or when a manager raises the limit. The model … has no known price, and this panel has a monthly limit. Pick another model in the chat. A manager can remove the limit, or allow a model with a known price. The AI provider answered with another model than the one allowed. Retry. If it happens again, tell a manager of the panel. This conversation got long: I summarized its first part to go on. Nothing: it goes on. This conversation is too long, even summarized. Start a new conversation. The assistant stopped unexpectedly. Retry. The panel's GitHub access cannot write to this repository. A manager saves a personal access token that can write to it in Settings → GitHub. This confirmation expired. More than ten minutes passed: ask for the action again.

docs.title: What goes to the AI provider
docs.text:
To answer, the assistant sends to the provider your panel uses — its name is in the first-use notice and in the label next to the message field:

  • your messages, and the screen you have open (the project, instance or server);
  • what its tools read: your projects' and instances' settings, jobs, logs, mail a staging caught, files of your repository, pages of the documentation and of the panel's public code.

With OpenRouter, the notice says so: what you send goes to OpenRouter and to the company behind the model chosen.

The panel's secrets — passwords, keys, tokens — never go: they are masked in everything the assistant reads, and the assistant cannot set them. Do not paste a password or a key into the chat: the panel masks its own secrets, not yours.

The key and the contract with the provider are your organisation's, and so is the cost: the provider invoices you, and the consumption the panel shows is only an estimate. What the provider does with what it receives is set by your contract with it; check it. IncubaCloud does not use your messages, your conversations or what the assistant reads to train AI models.

docs.title: What stays in the panel
docs.text:
• Conversations: 30 days after their last activity, then deleted. Only their owner reads them in the panel, also while the assistant is off; a manager does not. They are stored in the panel's database without encryption: whoever administers the server or the database itself can reach them. A deleted user's conversations go with them.
  • Actions: in the audit log, under the user's name, via agent Assistant (conversation N).
  • Usage: tokens and approximate cost per user and month, for the managers. It holds no message, so it stays when a conversation is deleted: deleting one does not give the month's limit back.
  • The box ticked to switch it on (on IncubaCloud SaaS, your acceptance of section 12A of the Terms): when, who and from where, at the moment the assistant was switched on.

docs.title: What it cannot do
docs.text:
• More than your role allows.
  • Change anything without your confirmation in the chat, except trying code on a staging; and after it read logs, files or mail others write, nothing at all until you write again.
  • Deploy to production on its own.
  • Read anything of the server outside the panel's public code and the documentation.
  • Follow instructions it finds in logs, files or mail: it treats them as data, and an action they ask for still needs your confirmation.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: What Limit Spending A monthly limit per user, set by a manager in euros (none by default). Approximate: it is checked before each call to the model, so one call in progress can take a conversation a little past it; a call that times out may be billed by the provider without the panel knowing, and the summary of a long conversation is counted, but the limit is not checked before it. A model with no known price counts only tokens, so it cannot be used under a limit. One task 30 steps unless a manager changed it (1 to 200); then it asks whether to go on. Your messages 20 a minute; one is cut at 20,000 characters. A confirmation Ten minutes, used once. A command in an instance 60 seconds. One commit 50 files and 180,000 characters. A conversation When it gets too long for the model, the assistant summarizes its first part and goes on, and says so. The messages stay for you. Panel code and documentation Read from the public repository of the panel only, 256 KB a file. Conversations kept 30 days after the last activity.

docs.title: Assistant settings
docs.text:
Managers set the assistant up in Settings → Assistant. It is off until you turn it on. Changes are kept with the page's Save changes.

Turned off, nobody can ask it anything. Its users keep their conversations, to read or delete them until they expire, 30 days after their last activity; the button stays for them meanwhile.

docs.title: Provider and key
docs.text:
The assistant uses your own key of an AI provider: Anthropic, or OpenAI, Google Gemini and OpenRouter (marked beta: not yet tested with the panel's tools). The panel talks to each provider at its own fixed address and to no other: there is no field for a web address. A self-hosted panel needs outbound access to the provider's address (and to GitHub's, for code).

Paste the key under Provider key and save: the panel lists the provider's models with it first, so a wrong key, or a panel that cannot reach the provider (a self-hosted panel without internet access), is told at once. The key is stored encrypted and never shown again; type a new one to replace it, or press Remove the key (the assistant goes off).

Every user the assistant serves uses this one key, each with their own role.

Changing the provider. A key belongs to one provider, so type the new provider's key in the same save. The models are the new provider's: the allowed models and the default one start empty and the assistant goes off: Assistant on cannot be ticked until the new key is saved. Choose the models, then switch it on as the first time, box included, and save. Everyone sees the first-use notice again, now naming the new provider.

docs.title: Switching it on
docs.text:
Assistant on needs a key, at least one allowed model and a default model, and a box ticked with it. The box is asked each time the assistant is switched on, and not again while it stays on. The panel records the date, who ticked it and from which address, and shows it under the form.

IncubaCloud SaaS

The box is I accept section 12A (AI features) of the Terms of Service, with a link to the Terms: they say what is sent to the AI provider, who pays for it, and which actions wait for confirmation. IncubaCloud records your acceptance on your account first, with the version of the Terms, and the panel shows it: Section 12A of the Terms accepted on … by … from … (terms of …). If it could not be recorded, the assistant stays off and the panel says so; try again later.

On a self-hosted panel there are no IncubaCloud Terms to accept. The box is I understand that what the assistant reads is sent to my AI provider, and that it can make mistakes, with no link. It is recorded in the panel only, without a version: Last switched on, with the box ticked, on … by … from ….

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
The list comes from the provider, with the key; Update the list reads it again. Choose the models your users may pick (Allowed), and the default one (Default). Recommended models were tested with the panel's tools; Untested ones may fail, mostly at writing modules.

Price unknown: the panel does not know that model's price. Without a monthly limit it can be used, and only its tokens are counted. With a limit it cannot: its cost could not be counted against the limit, so you cannot allow it (Not usable with a monthly limit), users see it disabled in the chat, and the default model must have a known price.

The panel asks the provider for the model chosen and no other: it never lets the provider fall back to another model, and an answer from a different one is set aside and recorded in the audit log. A conversation whose model is no longer allowed moves to the default one at its next message, and says so.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
Only the users you tick see the assistant. Choose them one by one; their role still decides what the assistant may do for them.

What asks for a confirmation is not a setting: the same rules hold on every panel (see the assistant). After the assistant reads text other people can write — logs, repository files, mail, a command's output — every change of that task asks the user, the work on its own new branch included, until the user writes again.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Monthly limit per user (in EUR): one value, the same for every user: what each user's conversations may cost per month, in euros, approximately (0: no limit). When a user reaches it, the assistant stops for them until next month or until you raise it. Each user sees their own spending in the chat.
  • Steps per task: calls to the model one task may make before it stops and asks whether to go on (30 by default, from 1 to 200).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: The table shows each user's tokens and approximate cost per month. Costs are estimates from the provider's public prices, in euros; your provider's invoice is what you pay. A row marked with * includes calls of models whose price is not known: only their tokens count.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text: Backups go to your own S3 bucket — AWS, MinIO, Backblaze B2, Wasabi, or any S3-compatible service. You hold the keys. We run the schedule and the encryption.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. You register a backup backend (your S3 endpoint + credentials + a passphrase).
  2. You attach the backend to a project (or set it as the global default).
  3. The platform runs a nightly backup on every production instance and uploads the encrypted bundle to your bucket.
  4. Manual backups are available any time from the instance detail.

The backup format is the standard Odoo dump (dump.sql + filestore/) wrapped in an encrypted archive.

docs.title: Backup destinations
docs.text: A destination (a backup backend) is a bucket and a key to it. A production instance cannot be deployed without one.

docs.title: Only S3-compatible storage
docs.text:
The only type is S3 compatible: AWS S3 or any service that speaks its API. Azure Blob Storage, a local disk, SFTP and FTP are not destinations. (An SFTP or FTP link is accepted in one place only: as the source of an archive to restore from a link.)

Each instance's backups are made on its host, by a backup container that runs duplicity. The panel also reads the bucket, to list the backups and measure their size, so the endpoint must be reachable from the hosts and from the panel.

docs.title: Create one
docs.text:
1. Create the bucket at your provider: the panel does not create it.
  2. Create a key that can list the bucket, and read, write and delete objects in it: backups write, the panel lists, the retention and the end of an instance delete.

  3. In the panel, Backup Destinations → New Backend: a Name on the General tab, then the Storage tab:

    Field What to put Bucket The bucket's name, nothing else. Path A prefix inside it, backups by default. Each instance writes under <path>/<project folder>/<instance>/. Endpoint URL Empty for AWS S3; the provider's S3 endpoint otherwise (below). Access key ID, Secret access key The key of step 2. Passphrase Read the passphrase first.

  4. Test Connection. It names what is wrong: the key (403), a bucket that is not there (404), or an endpoint other than the bucket's (301).

There is no region field: the panel and the backup container use the endpoint you give.

docs.title: Examples
Use it
docs.text: Choose the destination on an instance, on its project, or for every production instance in Settings → General → Default backup destination. An instance uses its own if it has one, else its project's, else the default.

docs.title: How long backups are kept
docs.text:
Every backup backend has a retention period (its Advanced tab) — 3 months unless you change it (30D, 3M, 1Y…) — and a retention owner, who deletes the backups older than that:

  • Duplicity cron (the default) — the instance's backup service deletes them.
  • Bucket lifecycle — a lifecycle rule you set up on the bucket, outside IncubaCloud, deletes them.
  • Nobody — nothing is deleted, and the archive keeps growing.

A manual backup of a production instance runs the same job as the nightly one, into the same bucket, and expires under the same rules.

IncubaCloud SaaS: the backup days in your plan

The backup days in your plan — 7 on Starter, 30 on Professional, Business and Agency, none on Free — are for the backups we take of your control plane, the panel at <subdomain>.incubacloud.io. They do not change how long your instances' backups are kept: that is always the retention of their backend.

docs.title: What happens to backups when an instance ends
docs.text:
Backups belong to the instance that made them, and they never outlive it.

You choose The instance Its backups Delete completely removed from the host and from the panel all destroyed, before the containers come down Archive removed from the host, kept in the panel exactly one copy kept, taken at that moment

There is no third option, and no "delete the instance but leave the backups": a chain nobody owns is one nobody can find, restore or prune, while it keeps consuming your bucket.

Archiving takes a fresh full backup first and prunes everything older, so the copy is from the moment you archived rather than from the last nightly run. That copy still counts against your bucket storage — you can see its size in the project's Archived tab — and it stays until you revive the instance or delete it.

Deleting cannot be undone

Both deleting an instance and deleting an archived one destroy the objects in your bucket. Download a backup first if you might need the data.

docs.title: Managed Backup Storage
docs.text:
IncubaCloud SaaS — paid add-on

If you'd rather not bring your own bucket, the platform can provision one for you: a dedicated bucket with its own scoped credentials, handed to you as a ready-to-use backup backend. Three tiers:

Tier Included storage Monthly Overage Starter 20 GB 2.99 € 0.05 €/GB Standard 100 GB 8.99 € 0.04 €/GB Pro 500 GB 29.99 € 0.03 €/GB

The bucket lives on Cloudflare R2 in the European Union, and the backups in it are encrypted with your passphrase before they leave the host — see Service limits.

Usage is measured periodically; storage beyond the included amount is billed as overage on your subscription invoice. Ordering a tier, or moving to a bigger one, charges your saved card right away for the days left in your current billing period, and it renews with your plan; an amount under 0.50 € is not charged at once, but added to your next renewal invoice. Cancelling the add-on or moving to a smaller tier takes effect at your next renewal; until then the storage keeps working as it is, and nothing is refunded. After a cancellation, backups are kept for a 30-day retention window before the bucket is purged. A smaller tier applies at the renewal only if your usage fits in it by then; otherwise you stay on your current tier and we tell you.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
Every backup is encrypted with the passphrase you set on the backend before it leaves the host. We don't store the passphrase in clear and we can't recover it. Treat it like a master key — store a copy in your password manager.

  • Type your own when you create the destination, and copy it to your password manager before saving. Left empty, the panel generates one and, like every secret it stores, never shows it again: the field only says that a value is set.
  • Why a copy outside the panel. Without the passphrase nobody can read the backups: not you, not the panel, not your storage provider. The day you need them most — the panel or the host is gone — the copies the panel and the host keep are gone with them.
  • Changing it later re-encrypts nothing: backups made before still need the passphrase they were made with (see Restore failed: passphrase mismatch).

docs.title: What lives where
docs.text:
• Bucket — your S3, encrypted bundles. We never see the raw data.
  • IncubaCloud database — backend metadata (endpoint, bucket, path). Credentials are encrypted at rest with the panel's key (INCUBACLOUD_SECRET_KEY on a self-hosted panel).

docs.text:
• Set up a backup destination
  • Restore a backup
  • Restore to any minute with continuous recovery
  • Receive an email when a backup completes (Backend detail → Notifications)
  • Override the project-level backend on a single instance (Instance detail → Settings → Backup backend)

A full per-screen reference for the Backup backend UI is coming soon.

docs.title: Restore to any minute
docs.text:
A nightly backup takes you back to last night. Continuous recovery takes a production instance back to any minute of its backup window: the database's changes are archived as they happen and the files copied as they change, so a mistake at 11:42 can be undone by going back to 11:41.

It lives in the instance's Backups tab, in the Continuous recovery card above the list of backups. It needs a backup backend, like the nightly backups, and uses the same bucket.

IncubaCloud SaaS

On the hosted service it comes with the plan: switched on by the platform with the plan's objective. The card shows the state and lets you restore; the objective is the plan's.

docs.title: What the card shows
docs.text: Field Meaning State OK · Archiving: everything is being archived. Behind: the archive is more than three objectives late; we are told, and it usually catches up on its own. Failing: nothing is being archived; we are told at once. Switching on… / Off. Restorable to The earliest minute you can go back to, and how many days are kept (the backup retention). The window grows from the moment it was switched on until it covers the retention. Last archived When the last piece of the database's log reached the bucket. Checked When the platform last asked the server. Last archived is as fresh as this: the check runs every ten minutes, so a reading a few minutes old is normal. Loses at most The recovery objective: how far behind the archive may be at worst, from 1 minute to 1 hour. Shorter means more frequent uploads. Changing it rebuilds the instance's stack, with a short pause.

docs.title: Restore to a moment
docs.text:
1. Open the instance, go to Backups and click Restore to a moment….
  2. Pick the moment, in your local time. It must be inside the window the card shows; the dialog opens on the present.
  3. Type the instance's name to confirm, then Restore.

What happens next, in order:

  1. A backup of the present is taken first, so the state you are leaving can be restored too.
  2. Odoo is stopped. Nothing of the instance runs meanwhile.
  3. The database is brought back to the moment chosen and the files with it. Whatever happened after that moment is undone.
  4. The restored database's modules are updated to the code the instance runs now, as a rebuild does (unless Auto-update modules on rebuild is off); the job's log names the branches and pinned commits.
  5. The instance is started again, and a fresh base copy is taken: the window now continues from the restored moment.

A restore does not change the code: to undo a deployment, revert its code first, or its migration runs again on the restored database. If the update fails, or has not ended within an hour, the instance still starts, on the database partly updated, and a warning names the module in the job's log: fix it and rebuild the instance.

How long it takes depends on the size of the database, usually a few minutes. The job's log shows every step; if the restored database does not come up, the previous data is put back and the instance started again, and the job says so.

Cancelling it. Cancel on the restore in Recent activity stops it where it is, the previous data is put back and the instance is started again; the job's log says so, usually within a minute. Once the restored database is up, the last step, the restore is no longer undone: it finishes, files and the update of its modules included, and the log says it had already been applied.

A restore undoes everything after the moment

Orders, invoices, messages, anything written after the moment chosen is gone from the instance, though it is still in the backup taken first. If in doubt, go back less far: you can restore again, to a later moment, from the window the card shows.

docs.title: Switching it on or off
docs.text:
Switch on rebuilds the instance's stack and restarts its database once; from then on it archives. The first base copy takes a few minutes, and the card says Switching on… until it is done.

Switch off stops archiving and lets the archive expire with the backup retention. The nightly backups go on as before.

docs.title: Restore a backup
docs.text:
Three flavours:

  • Download exact — full database with original users, crons, mail servers, credentials. For forensic recovery.
  • Download neutralized — same data, but crons turned off, mail servers archived, credentials scrubbed, and a red ribbon on top. Safe to load on a dev laptop.
  • Restore in place — replaces the live database of an instance with the chosen backup. Used to roll back a bad update.

docs.title: Pick the right mode
docs.text: If you're moving data to development or staging, download neutralized. If you're rolling back production after a broken release, restore in place. If you need a forensic copy with original credentials and crons, download exact.

docs.title: Download a backup
docs.text:
1. Open the instance and go to Backups. You see a chronological list of backups available in your bucket.
  2. Pick a backup, click Download.
  3. Choose Exact or Neutralized.
  4. The job starts and shows a progress bar.
  5. When ready, click the download link. You get a standard ZIP (dump.sql + filestore/), the same on every Odoo version from 8.0 to 20.0 — restorable on any Odoo of the same version.

docs.title: Restore in place
docs.text:
1. Open the instance and go to Backups.
  2. Pick the backup you want to restore.
  3. Click Restore.
  4. On production, you'll be asked to confirm twice. We want to be very sure.
  5. Wait for the restore to finish. The instance is briefly unavailable while the database is replaced. When the job ends in green, you're back online with the older data.

Before Odoo starts, the restored database has its modules updated to the code the instance runs now, as a rebuild does (unless Auto-update modules on rebuild is off); the job's log names the branches and pinned commits. A restore does not change the code: to undo a deployment, revert its code first, or its migration runs again on the restored database. If the update fails, Odoo stays stopped and the job says which module failed: fix it, dismiss the job's alert and rebuild the instance.

In-place restore is destructive

The current database is replaced by the backup. Anything created or modified after that backup's timestamp is lost. Take a fresh manual backup first if in doubt.

docs.title: Restore from an external ZIP
docs.text: A backup that did not come from here — an export from your previous provider, a dump a colleague sent you — can be restored the same way. Three routes, and the right one depends on where the file is and how big it is.

docs.title: From your browser
docs.text:
Open the instance → Restore Database → Through your browser, and pick the ZIP. Nothing to install: the file is sent in pieces, so it is not limited by the size a single request may carry, and a piece that fails is re-sent on its own. A progress figure tells you where it is.

The ceiling here is disk, not the network: the file waits on the panel's own storage until it is sent to the host. 2 GB by default; your administrator can raise it.

docs.title: From your computer, without a size limit
docs.text:
For a 20 GB database, or when you would rather not send it through the panel at all, use Through SSH. You do not need an account on the machine and you do not need to have a key of your own:

  1. Click Give me an upload key. We generate a key pair, install the public half on the host, and show you the private half once.
  2. Copy the command shown, put your file's name in place of <your-backup.zip> and run it. It writes the key with private permissions, sends your file as restore.zip, and removes the key afterwards.
  3. Click Check what arrived. The host reports the name, the size and the SHA-256 of the file it actually received — check it is yours.
  4. Click Import.

The key can only write into one directory on the host, cannot open a shell, and stops being accepted after twelve hours whether or not anyone remembers to remove it. The restore removes it as soon as it starts.

Windows

The command uses rsync, which Windows does not ship. On Windows use the browser route, or From a link below.

docs.title: From a link
docs.text: If the backup already lives somewhere reachable — your previous provider's download URL, an FTP or SFTP server, a pre-signed link from object storage — use From a link and paste the address. The host downloads it itself, so nothing passes through your connection or through the panel, and there is no size limit. https://, sftp:// and ftp:// are accepted, and a link carrying a user and password works too; the password is stored encrypted and never shown again.

docs.title: Bring an Odoo you run elsewhere
docs.text:
To move the data of an Odoo installed somewhere else — a package install, a container, another provider — into a new production instance:

  1. Check the three things a restore needs.
    • The same Odoo series as the database: a database of another version has to be upgraded first.
    • Every module the database has installed, available to the instance: put the repositories that carry them in the project (which modules a repository brings).
    • PostgreSQL of the source's major version or a newer one, chosen on the instance form's Database tab.

  2. Make the ZIP on the source.

    With Odoo's database managerBy hand, on the source server

    Open /web/database/manager, Backup the database with the format zip (the other one leaves the filestore out). For small databases: the download goes through Odoo's web server.

    mkdir odoo-export && cd odoo-export
pg_dump --no-owner --format=plain --dbname=<database> > dump.sql
cp -r <data_dir>/filestore/<database> filestore
zip -r ../odoo-export.zip dump.sql filestore

    <data_dir> is the data_dir of the source's Odoo configuration (~/.local/share/Odoo of the user Odoo runs as, when unset). Run pg_dump with the client of the source server's PostgreSQL.

    Either way, unzip -l shows dump.sql and filestore/… at the top of the archive, not inside another folder.

  3. Create the instance: a production instance in a project with those repositories and a backup destination. Deploy it: it comes up with an empty database, which the restore replaces.

  4. Restore Database, by one of the three routes above. On a panel or a host only your network reaches, use the browser or SSH: a link is fetched from the internet only.

The job stops Odoo, replaces the database and the filestore, installs the panel's sign-in module if it is missing, and starts Odoo again. The archive is loaded as a copy: the database gets a new unique id and a new secret, so it does not pass for the source database.

Nothing is switched off

The data comes back as it was: scheduled actions, outgoing mail servers, users. If the source installation still runs, both now send mail and run the same scheduled actions. Stop the source first, or switch them off on one side.

Before Odoo starts, the modules whose code differs from what the database last ran are updated to the instance's code, as a rebuild does, unless Auto-update modules on rebuild is off. If that update fails, Odoo stays stopped and the job names the module: fix it, dismiss the job's alert and rebuild the instance. Sign in with the users and passwords of the source database.

docs.title: Verify it worked
docs.text:
For downloads:

  • The ZIP opens and contains dump.sql + filestore/.

For an Odoo brought from elsewhere:

  • The instance opens on your data, attachments and images included.
  • Settings → Technical → Automation → Scheduled Actions shows the ones you expect active, and only those.

For in-place restore:

  • The instance is back up.
  • The data matches the backup's timestamp.
  • The job log ends in green.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Restore failed: passphrase mismatch

The backup was encrypted with a different passphrase than the one currently configured on the backend. Check Backend detail → Passphrase. If you've rotated passphrases, you need the original to read older backups.

The restore of an archive from elsewhere fails while loading it

Check the archive's layout first: dump.sql, in plain SQL, at the top of the ZIP, with filestore/ beside it (unzip -l).

The instance starts but Odoo fails on a module

A module installed in the database is not available to the instance: its repository is missing, or left out by the repository's Modules list. Add it and rebuild.

Restore failed: schema version mismatch

The backup was taken from a different Odoo version than the instance you're restoring to. Deploy a fresh instance with the matching Odoo version, then restore there.

The upload key expired before I finished

Ask for another one — they are single-use and cost nothing. Each key writes into a directory of its own, so the new command starts the upload from the beginning: what the previous key got across is not reused.

The link was refused

We only fetch from https, sftp and ftp, and only from an address that is reachable from the public internet. A link pointing at a private or internal address is refused on purpose: otherwise "restore from a link" would be a way to make our hosts read things they should not.

I want to restore to a different instance, not the source

Deploy a new instance, configure its backup backend to point to the same bucket, and the backup list will include the source's backups. Pick the one you want and Restore.
