Staging instances are not counted

Only production instances use up the allowance. Stagings — the test copies you clone from production, one per pull request or as many as you want to keep — run on servers you already pay for, so we do not charge a slot for them. Neither does the limit on extra instances below.

Annual billing is paid once a year and costs ten monthly payments: two months free. You choose monthly or annual billing at checkout. Changing plans keeps that billing period: an existing subscription cannot be moved between monthly and annual billing.

docs.title: Extras
docs.text:
If you need more capacity without jumping a tier, add extra hosts or instances from My account → IncubaCloud → Extras. Per unit and month:

Plan Extra host Extra instance Starter 3 € 1.50 € Professional 2.50 € 1 € Business 2 € 0.75 € Agency 1.50 € 0.50 €

Prices exclude VAT.

Free has no extras.

  • Adding one charges your saved card right away for the days left in your current billing period: the unit price for your billing period × days left ÷ days in the period. For example, an extra host on a monthly Starter subscription with 12 of its 31 days left costs 3 € × 12 ÷ 31 = 1.16 €, plus VAT. An amount under 0.50 € is not charged at once: it is added to your next renewal invoice. From then on it renews with your plan.
  • Removing one takes effect at your next renewal: you keep it until then, and it is not billed again. Nothing is refunded. One you are still using cannot be removed; free the host or instance first.
  • The price of extras follows your plan: after a plan change, your extras renew at the new plan's price.

docs.title: VPS billing
docs.text:
If you order a VPS through the platform, it is billed by the hour with a monthly cap: in a calendar month you never pay more than the monthly price the catalog showed you when you ordered it, and short-lived servers only cost the hours they ran. The price is Hetzner's list price excluding VAT, plus a management margin, the same on every plan: for the server and its IPv4 address, by the hour at Hetzner's hourly rate with the margin, and never more in a month than the monthly price. Your control plane shows the exact hourly and monthly price before you order. VAT is added on our invoice. The usage appears as a line on your subscription invoice. An ordered VPS does not use your plan's host allowance, so it never adds an extra-host line.

If you bring your own VPS, we bill nothing for it: it takes one host of your plan's allowance, or an extra host.

docs.title: Payment
docs.text: We use Stripe. Payment is by card; the card is saved (tokenized by Stripe) to charge the recurring subscription.

docs.title: Invoices
docs.text:
Invoices are generated automatically and stored under My account → Invoices. They're VAT-compliant for EU customers. What is charged at once — an upgrade, an extra, or Managed Backup Storage ordered, reactivated or moved to a bigger tier — gets its own invoice there, with the same taxes as your subscription invoices.

Prices are shown excluding VAT. Customers in Spain, and customers elsewhere in the EU without an EU VAT number validated in VIES, are charged Spanish VAT (21%); businesses elsewhere in the EU with a VIES-validated VAT number are invoiced under the reverse-charge mechanism; customers outside the EU are not charged VAT. Enter your VAT number in the billing address at checkout; we check it in VIES, and while the check is pending you are charged VAT. After your first order it can only be changed by us: contact us, and the change applies from your next renewal.

docs.title: Support
docs.text:
Support covers the management platform only — not Odoo functional consulting or custom-code support. Email support is at support@incubacloud.io, and the times are to our first reply:

Plan Support Free Documentation Starter Email, first reply within 3 business days Professional Priority email, first reply within 1 business day Business Email, first reply the same business day, plus live chat Agency Email, first reply the same business day, plus live chat
  • Live chat (Business and Agency) opens from your customer portal, My account, during business hours.
  • Business days are Monday to Friday, except public holidays in Barcelona (Spain). Business hours are 9:00 to 18:00, Madrid time.

docs.title: Changing plans
docs.text:
My account → IncubaCloud → Change plan, or from your control plane.

  • Upgrading — takes effect immediately: limits are raised on the spot, and your control plane may be briefly unavailable while the new plan is applied. Before applying it we show you what it costs, and your saved card is charged the price difference between the two plans for the days left in your current billing period: (new price − current price) × days left ÷ days in the period, with the same taxes as your subscription invoices. For example, moving from Starter to Professional on a monthly subscription with 12 of its 31 days left costs (39 € − 19 €) × 12 ÷ 31 = 7.74 €. An amount under 0.50 € is not charged at once: it is added to your next renewal invoice. From your next renewal the subscription bills the new plan's price. If the payment fails, your plan does not change and you are told so; update your card under My account → IncubaCloud → Payment method and try again. The price of extras follows your plan: after a plan change, your extras renew at the new plan's price.
  • From Free — moving from Free to a paid plan goes through checkout: the new plan applies once that payment goes through.
  • Downgrading — scheduled for the start of your next billing cycle; you keep the higher tier until then. You can cancel a pending downgrade at any time before it applies. Nothing is refunded when you downgrade, remove or cancel something: you keep what you paid for until your next renewal, and the change applies then.

Downgrading with too many resources

A downgrade is refused while you use more hosts or instances than the target plan allows; towards a paid plan you can choose instead to keep the excess as paid extras. A move to Free is also refused while you still have an on-demand VPS, active Managed Backup Storage or extras: release, cancel or remove them first.

docs.title: If a payment fails
docs.text:
We retry and notify you. If the subscription stays unpaid, the platform steps in progressively, counting from the day the payment was found overdue:

  • After ~7 days — on-demand VPS and Managed Backup Storage are released. A VPS is destroyed once a snapshot of its disk is taken; Managed Backup Storage keeps its bucket, but your access to it is revoked.
  • After ~14 days — your control plane is suspended: stopped, with its data kept.
  • After ~30 days — your control plane is deleted, together with those VPS snapshots and storage buckets. We keep one copy of the control plane for 30 days: see Coming back.

Paying before the deletion brings your control plane back and gives you access to your Managed Backup Storage again. A released VPS is not rebuilt for you: once you have paid, open it in your panel and use Restore server to bring its disk back from the snapshot. Servers you connected yourself are not touched at any step.

docs.title: An unused Free control plane
docs.text: A Free control plane nobody uses for 14 days is suspended; we email you three days before. You can reactivate it with one click from My account → IncubaCloud. If it stays suspended for 30 days it is deleted, with a reminder a week before. Free makes no backups of the control plane, so nothing is kept.

docs.title: Cancellation
docs.text:
You can cancel at any time from My account → IncubaCloud → Cancel subscription; only the owner of the account can. Before you confirm, the page lists what your account has — instances, servers, Managed Backup Storage and extras — so that you can download what you need first.

  • A paid plan whose current period is paid — your subscription is not renewed: you keep the service until the last day you paid for, and nothing is refunded. Until then you can undo the cancellation from the same page; while it is scheduled you cannot change your plan or buy anything. The next day we delete your control plane and its instances, every VPS you ordered through the platform (without a snapshot), your Managed Backup Storage and every backup we hold of them, and we keep no copy. The VPS hours and the storage over your tier up to that day, and any amount carried to your next renewal, are invoiced then and charged to your saved card; that invoice stays due if the charge fails.
  • Delete now — the same page can delete everything straight away; you type your subdomain to confirm. You give up the rest of the period you paid for and nothing is refunded; the VPS hours until then and any amount carried to your next renewal are invoiced.
  • Free, an unpaid period, or a control plane not running yet — there is no paid period to keep, so your account is closed and deleted at once. Any unpaid invoice stays due.

Servers you connected yourself, and backups you send to storage of your own, are not touched. A deletion you ask for cannot be undone, and nothing can be recovered afterwards. We email you when it is done.

docs.title: Coming back
docs.text:
After a cancellation you asked for, nothing is kept: sign in and pick a plan whenever you like to start again with a new, empty control plane.

When we remove the control plane of a paid plan for another reason — after non-payment, for example — we keep one copy of it for 30 days. The disk snapshot of a VPS released with it, the server's IPv4 address (when it could be held) and its firewall are kept for the same 30 days, then deleted. If you come back within that window, signing in and picking a plan offers you two paths:

  • Recover my data — we redeploy your control plane and restore that copy into it. Your subdomain, data and settings come back as they were at the moment of removal. Recovering needs a paid plan: Free has no backup service to restore the copy with. A VPS released with the removal is not rebuilt for you: open it in your panel and use Restore server to bring it back from its disk snapshot, with the same IP address when it could be held.
  • Start from scratch — a new empty control plane on the same subdomain. The copy is deleted, so this one asks you to type your subdomain to confirm.

After the 30 days the copy is destroyed and cannot be recovered. Plans without automatic backups (Free) have no copy to keep, so coming back always means starting fresh.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
Never set up a server or a domain?

From zero to Odoo in production goes step by step, from nothing to an Odoo your team signs in to: the server, the domain and its DNS, the backups, the first deploy and the mail. It explains each word as it comes up.

Three short guides that take you from zero to a running Odoo instance:

  1. Create your account — sign up, pick a plan, log in.
  2. Create your first project — group instances under a customer or product; optionally connect a Git repo.
  3. Deploy your first instance — pick a host, an Odoo version, the modules; watch it boot.

Each step is independent — if you already have an account, jump straight to step 2.

docs.title: What you'll need
docs.text:
• An account with one of the identity providers listed on the sign-up page, such as GitHub, to sign in with (hosted SaaS).
  • A payment method if you choose a paid plan (we use Stripe — card).
  • Optionally: a Git repo URL for your custom code.
  • Optionally: a VPS you already own (or order one through the platform on a paid plan).

docs.title: After get-started
docs.text:
Most users move on to:

  • Setting up backups so your data is safe.
  • Connecting your own VPS if you bring your own infra.
  • Migrating from Odoo.sh or from another host if you're moving in.

docs.title: Deploy your first instance
docs.text:
This guide walks you through deploying your first Odoo instance: picking a host, a Postgres version, the modules, and watching the deployment log in real time.

Prerequisites

  • A project (create one).
  • A host: either your own VPS or one ordered through the platform.
  • For production, a backup destination.

Before you create the first instance

  • Production comes first. A staging is a copy of production: until the project has a production instance, the staging section's + stays disabled. Deploy production, then use Clone to Staging, next to it in the project's side menu, for a staging with production's data.
  • Production needs a backup destination. Deploying one without any is refused (No backup backend configured for this instance). Register a destination first (Backups) and choose it on the instance, on its project, or for every production instance in Settings → General → Default backup destination.

docs.title: 1. Open the project and click Deploy instance
docs.text: A side panel opens with the deployment form. The same form is reused later for re-deploys, so it's worth getting comfortable with each field.

docs.title: 2. Pick the environment
docs.text:
• Production — the customer-facing instance. Re-deploys go through the safe-rebuild flow: if the new image fails its boot test, the previous version keeps serving.
  • Staging — a test copy of production: the project needs its production instance first. You can have many. Re-deploys are direct.

docs.title: 3. Pick the host
docs.text: Select one of your registered hosts. The platform checks capacity automatically and prevents over-provisioning. If your hosts are all full, order a new one or connect another.

docs.title: 4. Odoo and Postgres versions
docs.text:
The instance runs its project's Odoo version, which you pick in the project's form (Odoo version, when you create the project or later under its General tab): the panel offers 9.0 to 20.0, and a new project starts on the newest one (20.0) unless you pick another. The deployment form does not ask for it: a new instance takes its project's, and keeps it if the project changes later. The version influences which modules are available and which Postgres major versions you can pick under the form's Database tab: 12 alone for Odoo 9.0 and 10.0, 12 to 13 for 11.0 and 12.0 (13 by default), 12 to 16 for 13.0 and 14.0 (16 by default), 12 to 17 for 15.0 (17 by default), 14 to 18 for 16.0 to 19.0 and 16 to 18 for 20.0, with 17 by default on the last two ranges.

If your project has a connected repo with .copier-answers.yml, we pre-fill the project's version from there; you can still pick another in the project's form.

docs.title: 5. Pick modules
docs.text:
Either:

  • Pick from the catalog — the official Odoo modules for the chosen version, plus the OCA modules in our default repo set.
  • Use your own — modules from your project's repo. The repo URL was set when you created the project; you can override per-instance under Settings → Repository.

Both modes can be mixed. Our deployer composes a Docker image with everything you selected.

docs.title: 6. Optional: custom domain
docs.text:
Add app.example.com (or any domain you control) under Networking → Domains. Its certificate is Automatic by default: on a host your visitors reach directly, the deployer requests a Let's Encrypt certificate and wires up HTTPS. The other choices are described in Custom domains and certificates.

DNS must be in place

For Let's Encrypt, the domain's A or AAAA record must already point to the host's IP at the moment of deployment, otherwise the validation fails. Set the DNS first.

If you skip the domain, the platform generates a subdomain under its base domain for testing (on the hosted SaaS: <name>.<your-subdomain>.incubacloud.io).

docs.title: 7. Hit Deploy
docs.text:
A job starts, and the panel says so: Started: Deploy Instance. It shows up under Recent activity on the instance; click it to open the job log in a new tab and follow it live. You'll see the steps in order:

  1. Build image (1–3 min depending on dependencies).
  2. Boot test (production only) — clone the database to __ic_boot_test, run click-odoo-update, drop. If this fails, the deploy aborts before touching the live instance.
  3. Update modules in the live database.
  4. Bring up the new container.
  5. Cleanup.

When the job ends in green, your instance is up.

See the boot test stop a broken push while production keeps running: watch the 98-second video.

Another action already running?

An instance runs one action at a time. If something else is running on it, the deploy is not refused: it waits its turn — the panel says Queued behind …, and Recent activity lists it as Queued · N ahead — and starts by itself. You can cancel it while it waits. If the action ahead of it fails, the queue waits until you retry that action or dismiss its alert. See One action at a time.

docs.title: Verify it worked
docs.text:
• The job shows Done in green.
  • The instance card shows Running.
  • Clicking Open takes you to the Odoo login.
  • If you set a custom domain, browsing to it shows the same Odoo with HTTPS.

docs.title: What happens next
docs.text:
• Check that your production instance's backups run.
  • Add the rest of your team via Settings → Users.
  • Read about environments if you'll use stagings.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Build failed: pip install error

Usually a Python dependency missing for the Odoo version you picked. Check the build log; the failing line tells you which package. Add it to your repo's requirements.txt and redeploy.

Every deploy and rebuild re-reads the requirements.txt of each of your repositories that is not pinned to a commit, so a package you add there is installed on the next build without touching the project's dependency list. If that list already has the same package with a different version, the build stops and raises a dependency conflict alert instead — open it and pick which version wins.

Boot test failed

A migration script in your custom modules raised an error. Check the boot test log section. Fix the migration, push, redeploy. Production stays untouched.

HTTPS certificate not issued

Re-check DNS resolution: dig +short app.example.com should return the host's IP. Let's Encrypt has rate limits — retry after 1 hour if you hit them.

Instance running but Odoo errors on login

Open Logs from the instance detail. Most first-time issues are missing Postgres extensions or wrong Odoo version vs database version.

docs.title: Create your first project
docs.text:
A project groups everything that belongs to one customer or one product: its instances, its repositories, its environments. Every Odoo deployment in IncubaCloud lives under a project.

Why projects?

Projects let you reason about ownership, billing splits per customer, and environment promotion (staging → production). They also scope which team members can see what.

docs.title: 1. Open the dashboard
docs.text: From /cloud, click New Project at the top right. A side panel slides in with the project form.

docs.title: 2. Fill in the basics
docs.text:
• Name — your customer's name or the product name. Shows up in lists and breadcrumbs.
  • Description (optional) — a short note for your team.

docs.title: 3. Connect a Git repository (optional, recommended)
docs.text:
Paste an HTTPS or SSH URL. We auto-detect the project layout:

  • .copier-answers.yml → doodba layout. We pick up the answers (Odoo version, Postgres version, repos, addons) and fill defaults for you.
  • .gitmodules → Odoo.sh layout. We register the modules so your custom code is available at deploy time.

If you don't have a repo yet, skip this step. You can add it later from Project detail → Settings → Repository.

Private repositories

For private GitHub repos, install the platform's GitHub App (Settings → GitHub) — it grants repository access without sharing credentials — or store a personal access token in Settings → GitHub. A URL with a token inside it (https://<token>@github.com/your-org/your-repo.git) is refused: credentials never travel in the URL.

docs.title: 4. Pick a backup destination
docs.text: Backup destination applies to every production instance of the project, unless an instance sets its own. A production instance cannot be deployed without a destination: choose one here, on the instance, or for every production instance in Settings → General → Default backup destination. See Set up backups for the full walkthrough, and Before you create the first instance for what the first deploy needs.

docs.title: 5. Save
docs.text:
You land on the project detail page. The sidebar lists environments (none yet) and a button invites you to deploy the first instance.

Next: deploy your first instance

docs.title: Environments
docs.text:
Each project supports:

  • One production instance. The customer-facing one. Deploys here go through the safe-rebuild flow (boot test before swap).
  • Many staging instances. For test copies. They share configuration with production but use independent databases.

You can clone production data to a staging instance at any time (see Backups → Restore).

docs.title: Verify it worked
docs.text:
• The new project shows up in your /cloud dashboard list.
  • Opening it shows the sidebar and a Deploy instance CTA.
  • If you connected a repo, the project detail shows the detected layout.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Repo connection says \"unable to authenticate\"

Verify the URL works from your terminal first: git clone <your-url> /tmp/test-clone. If that succeeds, double-check the GitHub App installation covers this repository (or that the token is active).

Layout not detected

We look for .copier-answers.yml and .gitmodules in the repo root. If neither is present, we treat the repo as a generic codebase — you can still deploy, you just lose the auto-fill of versions and module list.

docs.title: Create your account
docs.text:
IncubaCloud SaaS

This page applies to the hosted service at incubacloud.io. On a panel you install yourself there is no signup: follow INSTALL.md and open /cloud.

This guide walks you through registering, choosing a plan, paying (if applicable), and reaching your own IncubaCloud control plane.

docs.title: 1. Pick a plan
docs.text:
Open the pricing page and click the button on the plan that matches your stage. There are five:

Plan Best for What you get Free Looking around 1 host, 1 instance; the control plane sleeps when idle and has no automatic backups Starter Freelancers & solo devs 3 hosts, 5 instances, 7-day control plane backups Professional Small businesses 10 hosts, 20 instances, 30-day control plane backups Business Mid-size companies & growing teams 25 hosts, 50 instances, 30-day control plane backups Agency Agencies running Odoo for many clients 100 hosts, 150 instances, 30-day control plane backups, its own server for your control plane (ready within 1 business day)

The backup days are for the backups we take of your control plane. Your instances' backups go to the backup backend you set up, and keep its retention — see Backups.

You can change plan later. Free has no card requirement.

On Free, the control plane sleeps

On the Free plan your control plane is suspended after ~30 minutes without traffic and wakes automatically on the next request (the first request after a nap takes a few seconds). The instances you deploy keep running. On paid plans the control plane runs 24/7.

A Free control plane nobody uses for 14 days is suspended until you reactivate it, and deleted after 30 days suspended. We email you before each step — see Billing.

docs.title: 2. Choose your subdomain and sign in
docs.text:
Enter the subdomain you want for your control plane (e.g. acme → acme.incubacloud.io), then continue with one of the identity providers listed on the page, such as GitHub. There is no email-and-password form and no separate verification email: your identity comes from the provider you pick.

Subdomain rules: 3–63 characters, letters/digits/hyphens (a DNS label). Reserved names (www, api, admin, …) are not available.

docs.title: 3. Complete payment (paid plans only)
docs.text:
We use Stripe; payment is by card, saved for the recurring subscription. The platform provisions your control plane as soon as the payment confirms — usually within a few seconds. On the Free plan this step is skipped and provisioning starts immediately.

Invoices are generated automatically and available under My account → Invoices on incubacloud.io. They're VAT-compliant for EU customers.

docs.title: 4. Open your control plane
docs.text:
When provisioning finishes you get your own IncubaCloud at https://<your-subdomain>.incubacloud.io. Log in with the same social account — tenant instances use IncubaCloud single sign-on.

Your dashboard at /cloud is empty. That's expected.

Next: create your first project

docs.title: Verify it worked
docs.text:
• https://<your-subdomain>.incubacloud.io loads and you can sign in.
  • The dashboard at /cloud opens without errors.
  • My account on incubacloud.io shows your plan (and, on paid plans, the subscription).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The subdomain I want is taken or rejected

Labels must be 3–63 chars and unique; a few names are reserved. Pick a variant (e.g. acme-erp).

Payment succeeded but my control plane isn't up yet

Provisioning normally takes under a minute. If it's still not reachable after a few minutes, contact us with the receipt id from Stripe.

Can my teammates log in too?

Yes — invite them from your control plane. Additional users join by invitation (there is no open signup on your instance).

docs.title: From zero to Odoo in production
docs.text:
This guide is for you if you want your company's Odoo running on the internet, under your own name, and you have never set up a server, a domain or a mail account for an application. It goes in order, from nothing to an Odoo your team signs in to, and explains each word the first time it comes up.

The other guides in Get started go faster and assume you know these things. If you already have a server and a domain, start with Create your first project.

docs.title: What you will end with
docs.text:
• An Odoo in production: the copy of Odoo your company works in.
  • Its address: a name under the panel's own domain to begin with, and your own, such as erp.example.com, when you want it.
  • Backups every night, encrypted, kept off the server.
  • Mail that leaves Odoo: invoices, quotations, password resets.

Plan for about an hour, most of it waiting: for the server to be created, for the first deploy, and for a DNS change to be seen everywhere.

docs.title: Words you will meet
docs.text: Word What it is Server (or VPS, host) A computer in a data centre, rented by the month or by the hour, where Odoo runs. In the panel it is a host. Domain Your name on the internet, such as example.com. You rent it from a registrar, usually for a year at a time. DNS The internet's address book: it turns a name such as erp.example.com into the address (IP) of a server. You change it where your domain is managed. DNS record One line of that address book. An A record sends a name to an IP address; a TXT record holds text that mail services read. Backup destination Storage outside the server where the nightly backups go. Without one, a production instance cannot be deployed. Instance One running Odoo. Production is the one your company uses; a staging is a copy for trying things without risk. SMTP server The service that delivers the mail Odoo sends. Your mail provider has one.

docs.title: 1. Get your panel
docs.text:
IncubaCloud SaaS

Create your account on incubacloud.io and pick a paid plan: ordering a server and the managed backup storage, used below, need one. Your panel opens at https://<your-subdomain>.incubacloud.io.

On a panel you install yourself, follow INSTALL.md and open /cloud.

docs.title: 2. Choose the server
docs.text:
The size of the server depends on how many people will use Odoo at the same time. Odoo's own deployment guide sizes a server by its workers, the processes that answer people's clicks:

  • at most two workers for each vCPU, plus one: (vCPU × 2) + 1;
  • about 325 MB of memory each, on average: Odoo counts 80% of light requests at about 150 MB and 20% of heavy ones at about 1 GB;
  • about 6 users at once for each worker, with one worker left for the scheduled actions (the crons), as in Odoo's own example.

A server runs as many workers as both its vCPUs and its memory allow, after 2 GB kept for the system, the database and the proxy. For the usual sizes:

vCPU RAM Recommended for up to Any Under 4 GB Tests only 2 4 GB 24 users at once 2 8 GB 24 users at once 4 8 GB 48 users at once 4 16 GB 48 users at once 8 16 GB 96 users at once 8 32 GB 96 users at once 16 32 GB 192 users at once 16 64 GB 192 users at once

Users at once are the people working in Odoo at the same moment, not everyone with an account: a team of 40 where about a dozen work in Odoo at the same time needs a server for 12. A staging on the same server shares those workers. It is a starting point: heavy reports, large imports or many websites ask for more. You can move an instance to a bigger server later, with Move to host on the instance.

IncubaCloud SaaS: order it from the panel

Go to Hosts and press Order new VPS. In How many people will use Odoo at once? type how many of you will work at the same time, then choose the Location: the size recommended for you is picked, and every size says how many users at once it is recommended for and its price. The DNS is done for you: the platform creates the server's record under its own domain, and you do not need a domain to start. While the panel has no backup destination, the order of the managed backup storage opens once the server is ordered: step 3 explains it. See Order a VPS.

With your own server, rent one with Ubuntu 22.04 or newer from any provider, of the size above, and follow Connect your own VPS. It needs a DNS record before the first deploy: step 6 says how.

docs.title: 3. Set up the backups
docs.text:
A production instance is not deployed without a backup destination: the backups of your company's data have to have somewhere to go before there is data.

IncubaCloud SaaS: managed backup storage

When the panel has no backup destination yet, Order VPS offers Set up managed backups next, ticked. Once the server is ordered, the next window shows the storage tiers with their prices: choose one and confirm it, and it becomes the panel's default destination. Nothing more to configure. Skipped, you can order it later under Backup Destinations. See Managed Backup Storage.

Otherwise, create a bucket at an S3-compatible storage provider and register it under Backup Destinations → New Backend, as Backup destinations explains, and choose it in Settings → General → Default backup destination.

Either way, the backups are encrypted with the destination's passphrase, and without it nobody can read them (why). The managed backup storage comes with one the panel generated and never shows. Before the first deploy, open it in Backup Destinations, and on its Storage tab type a passphrase of your own in Passphrase, keep a copy in your password manager, and save. On a destination of your own, type it when you create it. Changed later, it re-encrypts nothing: the backups made before still need the passphrase they were made with.

docs.title: 4. Create the project
docs.text: A project holds your company's Odoo: its production and its stagings. On Projects, press New Project, give it a name, and save. You do not need a Git repository: without one, Odoo comes with the modules you pick from the catalog. See Create your first project.

docs.title: 5. Deploy Odoo
docs.text:
1. In the project's side menu, press + next to Production.
  2. Give the instance a name, choose the server of step 2 as its host, and pick the modules you want to start with (Sales, Invoicing, Inventory…). You can add more later.
  3. Press Create Instance, and then Deploy.

The first deploy takes a few minutes; you can follow it in Recent activity. When it ends in green, the instance's address, a name under the server's domain, opens Odoo's sign-in page. Details in Deploy your first instance.

Every instance starts with the limits of a small team: Odoo with 2 workers, 2 GB of memory and 2 CPUs, and its database with 1 GB. Two workers serve about 12 users at once. Above that, raise them: on the instance's Resources tab, the Memory limit and CPUs of Odoo and of the database, and on its Config tab, workers (Odoo's rule of thumb: two for each CPU, plus one). They apply on the next Deploy. See Memory and resources.

docs.title: 6. Your own domain
docs.text:
You can work with the address the panel gave the instance. To use your own, such as erp.example.com:

  1. Find the server's IP address: on Hosts, open the server; it is its IP address.
  2. Open your domain's DNS where it is managed: usually your registrar's website, in a section called DNS, DNS zone or DNS records. If your domain uses another DNS service, the registrar says which.

  3. Add an A record:

    Type Name Value A erp the server's IP address

    The Name is the part before your domain: erp for erp.example.com. Some providers ask for the whole name instead. Leave the TTL as it is.

  4. Wait until it is seen. Usually a few minutes, sometimes an hour. A DNS lookup website, or dig +short erp.example.com in a terminal, shows the IP address once it is.

  5. Add the name to the instance: Networking → Domains, + Add domain, erp.example.com, and Deploy again. The certificate for HTTPS is requested by itself, which is why the record must be in place first.

Your own server

A server you connect yourself needs one more record before its first deploy: a wildcard record, * (or *.odoo for names under odoo.example.com), pointing to its IP address. It is the domain you give the host in Wildcard domain, and each instance gets a name under it.

More choices, such as certificates you already have, in Custom domains and certificates.

docs.title: 7. Mail that leaves Odoo
docs.text:
Odoo sends invoices, quotations and password resets by mail. In production, it delivers them through the SMTP server you set on the instance: Networking, fields SMTP host, SMTP port, SMTP encryption, SMTP user and SMTP password. A staging never sends mail to anybody (why).

  1. Get the values from your mail provider. Its help pages give the SMTP server, the port (usually 587, with STARTTLS) and how to sign in. Many providers ask for an app password or a sending account instead of your own password. With Microsoft 365, the mail relay can sign in with OAuth2 instead of a password: see OAuth2 with Microsoft 365.
  2. Fill in the fields and Deploy again.
  3. Add the records your provider gives you to your domain's DNS, as in step 6: usually an SPF record (TXT) and a DKIM record (TXT or CNAME). Without them, much of what Odoo sends ends in spam.
  4. Try it: in Odoo, send a quotation to an address of yours outside the company.

docs.title: 8. Before you open it to the team
docs.text:
• The instance shows Running and opens at your address with HTTPS.
  • The instance's Backups tab shows a first backup the morning after the deploy; Create Backup takes one at once (Set up backups).
  • The passphrase you typed on the backup destination is in your password manager.
  • A test mail arrived, and not in spam.
  • Your colleagues are invited: Odoo's own users are created in Odoo, under Settings → Users.

docs.title: Coming from another Odoo?
docs.text: If your company already works in Odoo somewhere else, do steps 1 to 4, and then follow Migrations instead of step 5: the project and the production instance are made from what you already have.

docs.title: Hosts
docs.text: A host is a server (VPS or physical) where instances run. You can connect your own VPS or order one through the platform.

docs.title: Two paths
docs.text:
• Connect your own — for any VPS you already have. Hetzner, OVH, DigitalOcean, AWS EC2, on-premises — anything that exposes SSH. Walkthrough
  • Order one through the platform (SaaS, paid plans) — we provision a Hetzner VPS, lock down SSH, configure the proxy and register it ready to use. Billed by the hour with a monthly cap. Walkthrough

docs.title: What we install
docs.text:
Once a host is registered and you run Full Setup, we deploy:

  • Docker + docker-compose (if missing).
  • Traefik as the network proxy. It terminates HTTPS and routes traffic to the right instance based on the domain.
  • Let's Encrypt cert manager. HTTPS is automatic when you add a custom domain.
  • The edge guard (~/traefik/dynamic/ic_guard.yml), which has Traefik refuse Odoo's public /website/info page on every instance. An instance can allow it (how).

The host stays under your control — root access is yours. VPS ordered through the platform are billed on your IncubaCloud subscription invoice.

docs.title: Hosts behind a CDN
docs.text:
A host can be reached by its visitors directly, or through a CDN or reverse proxy that answers for it. The General tab has a switch for this, and it decides three things:

  • Who counts as a visitor. With the switch on, the rate limit counts the client the CDN forwards; with it off, the address that opened the connection. Setting it on a host the world reaches directly is the mistake that costs most: a direct request carries no forwarded chain, so every visitor is counted as the same one and they all share a single limit.
  • Whether the origin may be reached at all. With trusted proxy ranges set, Only accept traffic from the proxies applied above refuses anything that did not come through them, so the host's address cannot be used to go around the edge.
  • Where the certificate comes from. A CDN terminates TLS, so the challenge a host uses to obtain its own certificate never reaches it. Such a host is given a certificate instead — an origin certificate covering the whole domain, which only ever has to satisfy the CDN. Domains left on the Automatic certificate switch to it by themselves on their next deploy, for the names it covers.

Order matters

Give the host its certificate and its trusted ranges before pointing the domain at the CDN, and refuse direct traffic only once traffic is actually arriving through it. The other order leaves the host answering nobody.

docs.title: The host's default certificate
docs.text:
Host detail → Traefik → Default certificate holds the certificate the host serves when a router has none of its own: what a CDN in front of the host connects to, and what a domain set to Existing certificate is served. Paste the full chain and its private key, then save.

  • A pair that cannot serve is refused with the reason: half of one, an unreadable PEM, a key protected by a passphrase, or a key that belongs to another certificate.
  • Once stored, the tab shows which names the certificate covers, when it expires and who issued it. The key is never shown again; leave its box empty to keep it, or clear the certificate to remove both.
  • Saving marks the host's configuration as not deployed. Push Trusted Proxy Settings (or Full Setup) ships it to the host.

On the hosted service the platform supplies the origin certificate to its own hosts behind the CDN; a certificate set on a host here takes precedence over it.

docs.title: Open a shell on a host
docs.text:
Host Shell, in the host's action bar, opens a terminal on the machine itself — not inside one instance's container — as the SSH user the host is registered with. It is there for the things a panel does not cover: looking at the disk, the Docker daemon or a system service.

  • Who can — Administrators only, the same role that can run Full Setup on the host. A Developer keeps the terminal of each instance, which stays inside its container.
  • What is recorded — who opened it, when, from which address and browser, and when it closed. What you type and what the server answers are not recorded, because a shell is where passwords get typed.
  • Limits — one open shell per person and host, and at most 3 opened per minute (tunable in Settings → Rate limits). A shell with no keystrokes for 2 minutes closes itself.

Everything you run there affects the whole server and every instance on it.

docs.title: Common tasks
docs.text:
• Connect your own VPS
  • Order a VPS through the platform
  • Check host health (Host detail → Check)
  • Whitelist external domains that may proxy through (Host detail → Whitelist). This is also the list a new staging on this host starts with — each staging then keeps its own, on its own Whitelist tab.
  • Audit who did what on the host (Host detail → Audit Logs)
  • Import an instance that was already running on the host (Host detail → Import Instance)

Reference page is in progress

A full per-screen reference for the Host detail UI is coming soon.

docs.title: Connect your own VPS
docs.text: Bring any VPS — Hetzner, OVH, on-premises — over SSH. We deploy the proxy and request HTTPS automatically.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A VPS with Ubuntu 22.04 or newer (Debian 12 also works).
  • SSH access for a user with passwordless sudo that can use Docker: root, or a user prepared as in The user the panel connects as.
  • Ports 80 and 443 free: Full Setup puts the proxy there (what it changes).
  • Outbound HTTPS from the VPS to Docker Hub, ghcr.io, GitHub and PyPI, and during Full Setup to Docker's and the distribution's package servers: the full list.

A server only your network reaches

For a host and a panel without public access — an office VM — see also Panel on an internal network: names, certificates, and what needs the internet.

docs.title: The user the panel connects as
docs.text:
The panel needs a user that can:

  • run sudo without a password — Full Setup installs packages and writes under /etc, and hardening checks sudo -n before it starts;
  • use Docker without sudo — deploys run docker compose directly, so the user must be in the docker group.

root meets both. For a dedicated user, run this on the VPS, with the public key the panel shows (step 3 below) in place of ssh-ed25519 AAAA...:

sudo useradd --create-home --shell /bin/bash incubacloud
echo 'incubacloud ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL' | sudo tee /etc/sudoers.d/incubacloud >/dev/null
sudo chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/incubacloud
sudo visudo -cf /etc/sudoers.d/incubacloud

# Created before Docker is: a Docker that Full Setup installs later
# already counts this user in.
sudo groupadd -f docker
sudo usermod -aG docker incubacloud

sudo install -d -m 700 -o incubacloud -g incubacloud /home/incubacloud/.ssh
echo 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA... incubacloud' | sudo tee -a /home/incubacloud/.ssh/authorized_keys >/dev/null
sudo chown incubacloud:incubacloud /home/incubacloud/.ssh/authorized_keys
sudo chmod 600 /home/incubacloud/.ssh/authorized_keys

Full Setup also adds the user to the docker group, but a group counts from the user's next login: add it beforehand, as above.

docs.title: 1. Open the hosts page
docs.text: Go to /cloud/hosts. Click Add Host.

docs.title: 2. Fill in connection details
docs.text:
• Name — whatever helps you remember it (e.g. customer-foo-prod).
  • IP address — the public IP works fine.
  • Port — the SSH port, usually 22.
  • User — root is fine; a user with passwordless sudo is also fine.
  • Login type — SSH Key (recommended) or Password. Hardening needs a key: it copies the user's authorized keys to the account it creates.
  • Wildcard domain — the domain your instances get their names under (example.com or *.example.com): each instance answers at a name such as myproject-prod.example.com. Point a wildcard DNS record (*.example.com) at the host's IP before you deploy.

docs.title: 3. SSH key (recommended path)
docs.text:
On the Connection tab, Generate a key for me is selected: the panel creates a key pair for this host and shows its public key, with a button to copy it. The private half stays in the panel, stored encrypted.

Put the public key on the VPS, as the user you entered:

  • if you have not created the server yet, paste it in your provider's SSH key field when you create it, then come back and fill in its IP address;
  • if the server already exists, run the command the panel shows under the key, which appends it to that user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys:
mkdir -p ~/.ssh && chmod 700 ~/.ssh && echo 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA... incubacloud' >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Keep this page open until you create the host: the key is saved with it. Once you have copied the key, the panel asks before you leave the page.

To use a key of your own instead, choose Upload my own private key and upload the private half in SSH private key. It must have no passphrase (the panel has no field for one).

The host's Connection tab keeps showing the public key, so you can copy it again later.

Create the host, then click Trust SSH Key in its action bar. Green = we got in, and the panel keeps the host's key to check it on every connection.

docs.title: 4. Run Check
docs.text:
This probes the host: kernel, distro, free disk, RAM, Docker presence. Anything missing shows up so you can decide whether to install it manually or let us run Full Setup.

The Check ends with a verdict on the host's status:

Status When What it means Compatible Linux, 10 GB free or more, every tool in place. Ready for instances. Degraded Under 10 GB free, or a tool missing. An alert says which. The instances already there keep running. With little disk, no new one is placed on it and a build may run out of space: free space. For a missing tool, run Full Setup. Unsupported Not Linux, or the Check could not reach or read the host. Nothing is deployed there.

The job fails only when the Check could not measure the host. Once 11 GB are free, the low-disk alert closes by itself within minutes; a Check closes it from 10 GB. Full Setup on a disk under 10 GB fails and leaves the host Degraded with the same alert.

docs.title: 5. Run Full Setup
docs.text:
We install Docker (if missing), drop in Traefik, wire up cert auto-renewal, and run a final probe. Watch the log to follow each step.

When it ends in green, the host is ready to receive instances.

docs.title: What Full Setup changes on the host
docs.text:
Every step checks before it changes anything, so running Full Setup again is a repair, not a reinstall.

Where What Packages Installs git, Docker CE (through get.docker.com), the Compose plugin, python3-pip, python3-venv, pipx, zip and logrotate, when missing. The user pipx installs copier (pinned), invoke and pre-commit in ~/.local/bin, added to PATH in ~/.bashrc; git config --global init.defaultBranch master if unset; the user joins the docker group. /etc/docker/daemon.json Only while no container exists: Docker's bridge at 172.17.0.1/16 and an address pool of 10.200.0.0/14 in /24 networks, so the host can hold many instances (each takes a network). Docker restarts. With containers running, it is left alone. ~/traefik/ The proxy: Traefik and a read-only proxy of the Docker socket, Compose project inverseproxy, publishing ports 80 and 443 (and 8082 on the loopback, for metrics). Its settings are the host's Traefik tab. /var/log/traefik/ The proxy's access log, rotated daily and kept 30 days. ~/globalwhitelist/ The proxies of the host's Whitelist tab (Compose project globalwhitelist): the names stagings may reach.

Each instance you deploy later lives in ~/<project folder>/<instance name>/ of the same user.

A web server already on 80 or 443

The proxy must own ports 80 and 443, and the panel has no setting to move it. With nginx, Apache or anything else bound there, Start Traefik fails. See what holds them with sudo ss -tlpn | grep -E ':(80|443)\s', and move that service to other ports or to another machine first.

Addresses your network already uses

Docker's networks on the host come from 172.17.0.0/16 and 10.200.0.0/14, and the host routes those ranges to its containers. If machines of your network have addresses there, the host cannot reach them. Check before you run Full Setup: the panel has no setting for these ranges.

docs.title: Hardening (optional)
docs.text:
The first time you trust a new host's SSH key, the panel offers to harden it. You can also do it at any time with Apply Hardening in the host's action bar; a host that has not been hardened shows Not hardened next to its name.

Hardening applies a security recipe on the host:

  • a non-root operator user when you connect as root, and SSH on a rotated port, key-only, with root login disabled at the end;
  • an nftables firewall that accepts only SSH, HTTP and HTTPS, with a cap of new connections per visitor's address (50 a second by default, set on the host's Advanced tab);
  • fail2ban: an address that fails SSH three times, or the Odoo login form ten times in ten minutes, is banned for an hour (the login ban is off on a host behind a CDN);
  • kernel sysctl hardening, automatic security updates (with a reboot at 04:00 when a kernel update lands), a hardened Docker daemon, journald limits and auditd rules, with the audit log kept for weeks.

Every instance also gets a stricter limit on its login endpoints (20 attempts a minute per address) on top of the general one, from its next deploy or rebuild. The proxy's access log is kept 30 days on the host.

Before you apply it:

  • It needs Ubuntu 22.04+ or Debian 12+, and root or a user with passwordless sudo.
  • Services installed directly on the server, outside Docker, stop being reachable from outside: the firewall only lets SSH, HTTP and HTTPS in.
  • The first run restarts Docker, a 5–10 second interruption for the instances already running there.
  • If the host has never been set up and you connect as root, choose Hardening + Full Setup: Full Setup then installs its tools in the new user's home instead of root's.
  • Who can open SSH afterwards: the dialog says it. A panel that knows its own address allows only itself and the host's allowed SSH IPs; tick Also allow my IP to add yours. A panel that does not know its address leaves SSH open to any address, key-only.

Afterwards the panel reaches the host as the operator user on the new port. Re-running it is safe: every step checks the host before it changes anything.

docs.title: DNS for HTTPS
docs.text: For Let's Encrypt to issue a cert when you deploy a domain on this host, the domain must already point (A or AAAA) to the VPS IP at the moment of deployment. Set DNS first, then deploy. A host the internet cannot reach never gets one this way: see Panel on an internal network.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Connection refused
  • Check the VPS firewall (ufw is most common): sudo ufw status.
  • Check the SSH service: sudo systemctl status ssh.
  • Confirm the public key is in that user's authorized_keys, not just root's. Mismatched users is the most frequent cause.
Docker install failed

Most often a kernel too old for the modern Docker engine. Upgrade Ubuntu to 22.04+ or Debian to 12+. We don't support older kernels.

Full Setup gets stuck on Traefik

Check that ports 80 and 443 are free on the host (no nginx, apache, or other webserver running): sudo ss -tulpn | grep -E ':80|:443'. If something is bound, stop it first.

Full Setup fails on Docker with permission denied on its socket

The user is not in the docker group for this connection yet: add it as in The user the panel connects as, and run Full Setup again.

Hardening refuses to start: sudo asks for a password

The user needs NOPASSWD in its sudoers line.

docs.title: Order a VPS through the platform
docs.text:
IncubaCloud SaaS — paid plans

On-demand VPS ordering is available on the hosted service, on paid plans (Starter and up). Self-hosted deployments and Free-plan accounts connect their own VPS instead.

Order a Hetzner Cloud VPS without leaving IncubaCloud. The platform creates the server, locks SSH down to the platform, installs Docker and the proxy, and registers it as a host ready to receive instances.

docs.title: Pricing
docs.text:
VPS usage is billed by the hour with a monthly cap: in a calendar month you never pay more than the monthly price the catalog shows when you order, and short-lived servers only cost the hours they ran. The charge appears as a line on your subscription invoice. The price is Hetzner's list price excluding VAT, plus a management margin, the same on every plan: for the server and its IPv4 address, by the hour at Hetzner's hourly rate with the margin, and never more in a month than the monthly price. VAT is added on our invoice.

An ordered VPS does not use your plan's host allowance, which counts the servers you connect yourself, so it never adds an extra host (see Billing → Extras).

docs.title: 1. Open your Hosts dashboard
docs.text: In your control plane, go to /cloud/hosts and click Order VPS.

docs.title: 2. Pick size and location
docs.text:
The catalog (sizes, locations, live availability) comes straight from Hetzner. Each size shows the exact hourly and monthly price for the location you pick, before VAT, and that is what you will pay. Pick a region close to your users — EU (Helsinki, Nuremberg, Falkenstein) or US (Ashburn, Hillsboro).

Each size also says how many users at once it is recommended for, or that it is for tests only. Type the number of people who will work in Odoo at the same time in How many people will use Odoo at once?, and once a location is chosen the cheapest size recommended for them is picked for you; a smaller one says so under the list. The figure follows Odoo's own formula, explained in From zero to Odoo.

docs.title: 3. Choose the hostname
docs.text: If the platform manages your DNS, the new host gets a name like vps1.<your-subdomain>.incubacloud.io automatically. You can point your own DNS at it later for custom domains.

docs.title: 4. Confirm
docs.text:
If the panel has no backup destination yet, Set up managed backups next is ticked under the size: a production instance cannot be deployed without one. Once the server is ordered, the next window offers the managed backup storage with each tier's price, and none chosen. Choose one and confirm it to order it, and it becomes the panel's default destination; Skip orders nothing.

Provisioning takes a couple of minutes end to end:

  1. Create the server at Hetzner.
  2. Generate an SSH keypair and lock SSH to key-only access, firewalled to the platform.
  3. Install Docker and Traefik (Full Setup) and harden the host.
  4. Run the health probe.

When the job ends in green, the host shows up in your list, ready for deploys.

Monitoring. The server sends its metrics to the platform on port 9443. If you restrict its outbound traffic, allow that port.

docs.title: Cancellation
docs.text: Open the host, and delete/release it from the host actions. Billing stops with the hourly meter; the subscription invoice reflects only the hours used (never more than the monthly cap).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Ordering is refused on my plan

The Free plan cannot order on-demand VPS. Upgrade to a paid plan or connect your own server. On a paid plan, ordering needs a card saved for your subscription and no unpaid invoices: add the card under My account → IncubaCloud → Payment method, or pay the invoice under My account → Invoices, and order again.

Provisioning failed: out of capacity

Hetzner sometimes runs out of stock in a specific region for a specific size. Retry with a different region — failed provisions are not billed.

Provisioning failed: rate limit

Hetzner enforces creation rate limits. Wait 5 minutes and retry.

I want extra storage or a snapshot service

Out of scope today. Use the host's local disk plus backup backends pointed at S3 — same outcome, portable across providers.
