docs.title: Panel on an internal network
docs.text:
A self-hosted panel and its hosts can live on a network the internet does not reach: a VM in your office, a server behind a VPN. Most of the panel works the same there. This page covers what does not: names and certificates for the instances, AI agents, and the features that need a way in from the internet.

Installing the panel itself is in the repository's INSTALL.md; preparing a host, in Connect your own VPS.

docs.title: What needs the internet
docs.text:
Feature On an internal network Let's Encrypt certificates The host's proxy proves each name to Let's Encrypt through a connection to its port 443, which never arrives. Use a certificate you obtain yourself: Certificates. Rebuild on push, pull request previews They start from GitHub's notifications, which cannot reach a private address: Auto-rebuild never fires. Deploy and Rebuild by hand after a push; both work. Custom connectors in Claude (claude.ai and the Claude apps) Claude calls them from Anthropic's servers, which need a public HTTPS address. Connect a client that runs on your computer instead: AI agents. Restore from a link The host only downloads from public addresses. Restore through the browser or over SSH.

The hosts still need outbound HTTPS:

  • container images from Docker Hub (Traefik and its socket proxy) and from ghcr.io (Tecnativa's Odoo, PostgreSQL, backup and egress images), whose layers come from pkg-containers.githubusercontent.com;
  • code from GitHub (your repositories, OCA's and the doodba template) and Python packages from PyPI;
  • during Full Setup, also get.docker.com and download.docker.com (Docker's install script and packages) and the distribution's apt mirrors;
  • with host monitoring, its agents' images from Docker Hub, quay.io and gcr.io.

docs.title: Names: the wildcard domain
docs.text:
Host → Traefik → Wildcard domain is the domain the host's instances are named under when you give them no name of your own. Write it with or without the leading *.: *.odoo.example.com and odoo.example.com mean the same.

Name For <project folder>-<instance name>.odoo.example.com An instance created without a domain: the panel adds this row to its Networking → Domains. Without a project folder, <instance name>.odoo.example.com. traefik.odoo.example.com The proxy's dashboard, behind the host's Panel password.

The panel creates no DNS records. On your network's DNS server, point the whole domain at the host — one wildcard record, *.odoo.example.com → 192.0.2.20, or with dnsmasq:

address=/odoo.example.com/192.0.2.20

An instance can also answer to names outside the wildcard domain (Networking → Domains); each needs its own DNS record, and a certificate that covers it.

docs.title: Certificates
docs.text:
Each domain row has a Certificate choice (what each one does). On a host the internet cannot reach:

Certificate On an internal network Automatic (default) Resolves to Let's Encrypt, as the host is not behind a CDN, and gets no certificate. Let's Encrypt Gets no certificate. Existing certificate Serves the certificate the host holds, its default certificate. The one to use. No TLS Not plain HTTP: the proxy still redirects to HTTPS, and visitors get a self-signed certificate.

docs.title: When the certificate does not cover a name
docs.text:
The deploy log says, per domain, what it got:

  • TLS for app.odoo.example.com: host's certificate — covered.
  • ⚠ app.odoo.example.com: the host's certificate does not cover this name; browsers will warn. — the deploy goes on, and the host serves its certificate for a name it does not cover: browsers show a warning.
  • These domains ask for the host's certificate and the host holds none — the deploy stops before touching the host. Load a certificate first.

A wildcard certificate for *.odoo.example.com covers every name one level under it — all the names the panel generates — but not odoo.example.com itself, nor a.b.odoo.example.com.

docs.title: A wildcard certificate by DNS, with Cloudflare
docs.text:
Let's Encrypt can check that a domain is yours through a TXT record in its public DNS instead of a connection to your server (the DNS-01 challenge), and it issues wildcards only that way. The host's proxy does not do it for you: you obtain the certificate on any machine with Docker and internet access, and load it on the host. The domain must be a zone in your Cloudflare account; the records your network uses can stay on your internal DNS.

1. A Cloudflare API token. In Cloudflare, My Profile → API Tokens → Create Token, with the permission Zone → DNS → Edit, for that zone only.

2. Ask for the certificate. On that machine:

mkdir -p ~/certbot
printf 'dns_cloudflare_api_token = %s\n' '<your token>' > ~/certbot/cloudflare.ini
chmod 600 ~/certbot/cloudflare.ini

docker run --rm -v ~/certbot:/etc/letsencrypt certbot/dns-cloudflare:v5.9.0 \
  certonly --dns-cloudflare \
  --dns-cloudflare-credentials /etc/letsencrypt/cloudflare.ini \
  -d 'odoo.example.com' -d '*.odoo.example.com' \
  -m admin@example.com --agree-tos --non-interactive

The chain and its key land in ~/certbot/live/odoo.example.com/: fullchain.pem and privkey.pem.

3. Load it on the host. Host → Traefik: paste fullchain.pem under Default certificate and privkey.pem under Default certificate key, and save. The tab then shows the names it covers and when it expires. Push Trusted Proxy Settings (or Full Setup) ships it to the host.

4. Switch the domains. On each instance, Networking → Domains, set Certificate to Existing certificate — the row the panel generated included — and rebuild or deploy the instance.

Nothing renews it

A certificate loaded this way is renewed by neither the panel nor the host. Before the expiry date the Traefik tab shows, run the same container with renew in place of certonly …, paste the new pair and push it again; the instances need no rebuild.

The same steps load a certificate from your own certificate authority or one you bought: on an internal network, any certificate your users' browsers trust will do. Several certificates on one host are loaded by hand: RB-12.

docs.title: AI agents
docs.text:
An agent works on the panel through its MCP address, as you, with your role (Agents). On an internal network, connect it from a client that runs on your own computer, with an API key.

1. The MCP address. Settings → Agents (MCP) → MCP address is the address the Connect an agent page puts in its commands. Left empty, it is the panel's own address (web.base.url) followed by /mcp, and Odoo rewrites that address each time a user with access to Odoo's Settings signs in: it becomes the one in that user's browser, http://localhost:8069 after a sign-in through an SSH tunnel, for instance. Set the address your computers use, for example http://192.0.2.10/mcp; or set web.base.url to the panel's address and add the system parameter web.base.url.freeze with the value True, which stops the rewrite. Plain http is accepted for the MCP. Connecting the GitHub App needs the panel served over HTTPS, with any certificate your browsers trust; over plain HTTP the panel refuses it.

2. An API key, created in your Odoo preferences: Self-hosted panel without OAuth.

3. Claude Desktop through mcp-remote. Claude Desktop starts local MCP servers from its configuration file, and mcp-remote is one that relays to a remote address with a header on every request. It needs Node.js (npx) on the computer. In Claude Desktop, Settings → Developer → Edit Config opens claude_desktop_config.json; add:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "incubacloud": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "mcp-remote",
        "http://192.0.2.10/mcp",
        "--allow-http",
        "--header",
        "Authorization:${AUTH}"
      ],
      "env": {
        "AUTH": "Bearer <API_KEY>"
      }
    }
  }
}
  • --allow-http: without it mcp-remote refuses plain http to anything but your own machine. The key then travels unencrypted: use it only on a network you trust, and drop the flag once the panel is behind HTTPS.
  • Authorization:${AUTH} has no space after the colon on purpose; mcp-remote fills in ${AUTH} from env, where the space of Bearer <API_KEY> is safe. --header-file reads the header from a file instead.

Restart Claude Desktop. Other clients that run on your computer — Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Codex — connect to the address directly and send the key as a header: the commands are on the Connect an agent page.

4. Approvals. Every command an agent wants to run on a server or on a production instance, and every deletion or restore, waits for you, showing the exact command. You answer in the client, or open the link the agent gives you in a browser signed in to the panel. See Approvals.

docs.title: Verify it worked
docs.text:
openssl s_client -connect app.odoo.example.com:443 -servername app.odoo.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -subject -dates
  • The issuer is Let's Encrypt (or your authority) and the dates are the ones the Traefik tab shows; TRAEFIK DEFAULT CERT means no certificate on the host covers the name.
  • Asked to list your projects, the agent answers with them.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: What you see Why, and what to do The agent gets 401 The key is wrong, revoked or expired, or Bearer is missing in AUTH. 404 on /mcp Odoo cannot tell which database the request is for: select the panel's database by name, with db_name or dbfilter = ^<name>$ (INSTALL.md). mcp-remote refuses the http:// address Add --allow-http. The commands on Connect an agent name localhost:8069 Set the MCP address (step 1). A push does not rebuild the instance Expected without public access: rebuild by hand.

docs.title: Instances
docs.text:
An instance is a running Odoo deployment — one container, one database, one filestore. It belongs to a project and runs on a host.

Before you create the first instance

  • Production comes first. A staging is a copy of production: until the project has a production instance, the staging section's + stays disabled. Deploy production, then use Clone to Staging, next to it in the project's side menu, for a staging with production's data.
  • Production needs a backup destination. Deploying one without any is refused (No backup backend configured for this instance). Register a destination first (Backups) and choose it on the instance, on its project, or for every production instance in Settings → General → Default backup destination.

An instance's environment is chosen when it is created and cannot be changed later.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
• Production instance — customer-facing. Re-deploys go through the safe-rebuild flow (boot test before swap). One per project.
  • Staging instance — test copy. Re-deploys are direct. As many as you like: stagings run on servers you already pay for, so they never count against the instance allowance of a SaaS plan.
  • Odoo version — one the panel offers, 9.0 to 20.0, taken from the project when the instance is created and fixed once it is deployed. Odoo 20.0 runs on PostgreSQL 16 to 18; 16.0 to 19.0, on 14 to 18; 13.0 to 15.0, on 12 up to 16 or 17; 11.0 and 12.0, on 12 to 13; 9.0 and 10.0, on 12 alone.
  • Sleeping (SaaS Free plan) — on Free it is your control plane, not your instances, that is suspended after ~30 minutes without traffic to save resources. It wakes up on the next request (the first request after a nap takes a few seconds). The instances you deploy keep running.

IncubaCloud SaaS

Instances on the hosted service are served through a CDN, which caps a single request at 100 MB and at 100 seconds to first byte. See Service limits for what to use instead when you hit either one.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
deploy → running → rebuild → running → ... → archive or delete

A rebuild updates the image and modules without downtime (production) or restarts the container (staging).

docs.title: One action at a time
docs.text:
An instance runs one action at a time — deploy, rebuild, restart, backup, restore and the rest. Press a button while another action is running and the new one is not refused: it waits in the instance's queue and starts by itself when the one ahead of it ends, in the order they were asked for.

  • The panel tells you which: Started: Rebuild Instance, or Queued behind Deploy Instance.
  • Recent activity lists a waiting action as Queued · N ahead: how many actions start before it.
  • Queued · waiting for a free slot (root.user 1/1) means nothing runs on the instance, but the panel already runs as many actions as it runs at once (here one of one). It starts as soon as one of them ends.
  • Running · on the server, reconnecting at 12:03:05 means a long step, such as building the image of a rebuild, goes on on the server while the panel steps away and comes back for it at that time. Nothing to do: the action is running, and Cancel still stops it.
  • Changed your mind? A waiting action has not started yet, so Cancel takes it out of the queue at once and nothing happens on the server.
  • Asking twice for the same thing while it waits — two restarts, the same backup — does not queue it twice. A queue holds five actions at most.

After a failure, the queue waits for you

When a deploy, rebuild, restore or delete fails, what is queued behind it does not start: a restart after a broken deploy would only fail again. The waiting actions show Action required, which leads to the failure's alert. Retry the failed action — once it succeeds the queue moves on — or dismiss the alert in Alerts to let the queue go on as it is. With Auto-rebuild, a rebuild that failed does not stop the next push: pushing the fix rebuilds the instance, and once that rebuild succeeds the alert closes by itself.

Deleting an instance does not wait for the actions queued on it: they are cancelled, and the deletion starts as soon as the action running now ends.

Every action has a log. Click it in Recent activity (or in View all activity) to open its log in a new tab; a button never opens one by itself.

docs.title: Ending an instance
docs.text:
Both endings remove the containers, the database and the files from the host. They differ in what happens to the backups.

Deleting destroys the backups too

An instance's backups belong to that instance. Delete completely empties them before the containers come down — there is no option to keep them, and nothing to restore from afterwards. If you might want the data later, archive instead, or download a backup first.

Because it cannot be undone, the panel asks you to type the instance name.

Archive keeps one restorable copy. A fresh full backup is taken at that moment — not the last nightly one, so nothing since it is lost — and everything older is pruned, leaving exactly one copy. The instance moves to the Archived tab of its project, where you can see the size of that copy and when it was last verified.

From there you can:

  • Revive it — deploy it again, on the original host or any other, and restore the copy into it.
  • Delete it — which destroys the copy as well, and again asks for the name.

An archived instance keeps its name reserved inside its project: creating a new instance with that name is refused, because it would compute the same backup path and write into the copy being kept.

Archiving without a backup destination

An instance with no backup backend has no copy to keep, so archiving it keeps only the record. The panel says so and asks you to confirm in writing.

docs.title: Common tasks
docs.text:
• Deploy your first instance
  • Rebuild after pushing changes to your repo (Instance detail → Rebuild)
  • View logs (Instance detail → Logs). Odoo's log is kept one file per day and survives rebuilds: pick a day, search every day at once, or download one
  • Open a shell on the container (Instance detail → Shell)
  • Size its memory and CPU (Instance detail → Resources), and what the panel derives from them
  • Restore from a backup
  • Refresh a staging with production data
  • Get a preview instance for every pull request
  • Keep a staging that is about to expire
  • Add a custom domain (Instance detail → Networking → Domains)

docs.title: Custom domains and certificates
docs.text:
Instance detail → Networking → Domains lists the names the instance answers to. Leave it empty and the platform generates one under the host's wildcard domain. Each row has an optional redirect target (with 301 for a permanent redirect) and a Certificate choice:

Certificate What happens Automatic (default) The host decides. If a CDN answers for the name and the certificate the host holds covers it, the host serves that one; otherwise it asks Let's Encrypt. Pick this unless you have a reason not to. Let's Encrypt Always asks Let's Encrypt, whatever the host. The domain's DNS must point straight at the host when it deploys. Existing certificate Serves a certificate already on the host — its default certificate (Host detail → Traefik), or one loaded by hand. Use it for a purchased wildcard or a certificate from your own CA. No TLS No TLS for this name. The host still redirects HTTP to HTTPS, so in practice visitors get a self-signed certificate.

Changes take effect on the next deploy or rebuild. The deploy log says, one line per domain, how each name got its certificate — for Automatic, which way the host decided:

TLS for app.example.com: automatic → Let's Encrypt

Existing certificate needs a certificate

A deploy that asks for Existing certificate on a host holding none stops before touching the host and names the domain. Load the certificate first; the steps are in RB-12.

docs.title: Refresh from production
docs.text:
Instance detail → Refresh from production replaces a staging instance's database and filestore with a copy of its project's production, keeping the staging's own code (repositories and branches) untouched. It is the button you press when your test copy has drifted away from real data.

Two data sources:

  • Latest backup (recommended) — restores the most recent snapshot from the production's backup destination. No extra load on production.
  • Live dump from production — dumps the production database on the spot, so you get the data as of right now. It costs a pg_dump on a live database, and it is the only option when the production has no backup destination configured (the dialog then picks it for you).

Neutralize the database is on by default: the restored copy comes up with scheduled actions and outgoing mail servers disabled and Odoo's test banner showing. Leave it on unless you are deliberately testing a cron or a mail flow — a staging carrying production's data will otherwise invoice, dun and email your real customers. A rebuild that updates the modules of a neutralized staging or preview neutralizes it again afterwards, and its mail goes back to the staging's mail catcher: the update switches on again the scheduled actions its modules ship. A database without Odoo's test banner is left as it is.

The refresh runs as two jobs (a download on the production, a restore on the staging) that you can follow in the activity timeline. If the download fails the restore never starts and the staging is left untouched. Refreshing updates the modules to the staging's code before it starts, unless Auto-update modules is off; if that update fails, the staging stays stopped and the job says so.

Cloning a production to a new staging (Project → Clone to staging) applies the same neutralization, and always takes a live dump: a production created today has no backup to copy until its first nightly run.

docs.title: Auto-update
docs.text:
If you push commits to a connected repo, two settings control what happens:

  • Auto-rebuild — trigger a rebuild automatically when commits land on the connected branch. Off by default.
  • Auto-update modules — during rebuild, run click-odoo-update to update only the modules whose checksum changed. On by default.

Both live under Instance detail → Networking.

Auto-rebuild acts on GitHub's push notifications, which reach the panel through the GitHub App, and on GitLab's webhooks, so the panel must be reachable from the internet.

IncubaCloud SaaS

On the Free plan the control plane sleeps after 30 minutes without use, and a push notification of GitHub or GitLab that arrives while it sleeps only wakes it: the push is not acted on. Rebuilding on push needs a paid plan, whose control plane never sleeps; on Free, rebuild by hand.

docs.title: Pull request previews
docs.text:
A project can create a throwaway staging for every pull request, so a change can be looked at running — on real data — before it is merged. It is off by default; turn it on under Project → Settings → Preview instances for pull requests and merge requests. GitLab merge requests get previews the same way: see Merge request previews.

With it on, opening (or reopening) a pull request on a repository that one of the project's production instances follows does this, with nobody pressing anything:

  1. A staging named pr-<number> is created on the same host as that production, following the pull request's branch.
  2. It receives a copy of the production's data as it is at that moment — a live dump, so it works even before the first backup — neutralized exactly like Refresh from production: scheduled actions and outgoing mail servers disabled, test banner showing.
  3. It gets an address of its own under the host's wildcard domain (<project>-pr-<number>.<host domain>), and the panel comments that link on the pull request once the preview is up.
  4. Every new push to the pull request rebuilds it.
  5. Closing or merging the pull request deletes it, comment included.

Things worth knowing before switching it on:

  • A preview is a full copy of production data sitting on your host for as long as the pull request stays open. Anyone who can reach its address and log in sees that data.
  • It needs the GitHub App connected to the repository: the webhook that announces the pull request, and the comment, both go through it.
  • A production instance that pins the repository to a fixed commit does not get previews for it — a pin says "this instance does not move with the branch".
  • If a preview cannot be created, the pull request gets a comment saying why and the production instance an alert. Fix the cause, then close and reopen the pull request to try again.
  • The copy's modules are updated to the pull request's code before it starts. If that update fails, the preview stays stopped and the comment says it could not be updated; push a fix to the branch and its rebuild brings it up. If the update never ended (the connection to the server dropped or it ran out of time), it may still be running: a push rebuilds the preview only once the restore's alert is dismissed.
  • The panel acts on the pull requests of one installation of its GitHub App, the one under Settings → GitHub. If the App is installed on another account too, a pull request there gets no preview: the production that would have been copied gets an alert naming the account instead. Choosing that installation resolves it, or dismiss it.

docs.title: Stagings expire when nobody uses them
docs.text:
A staging that nobody has touched for 90 days is deleted automatically. Production instances are never affected.

The clock measures use, not age: a staging somebody opens every week never expires, however old it is. Two things reset it to zero:

  • You did something with it from the panel — deployed, rebuilt, restarted, restored, refreshed it, connected as a user, or opened a shell on it.
  • Somebody logged into its Odoo. The panel reads the last login from the staging's own database once a day.

Two things deliberately do not count. Rebuilds triggered by a push are code arriving, not a person looking at it. And the health probes that run every few minutes are the platform watching, not you.

A staging has no backup to go back to

Deletion removes the containers, the database and the files. Unlike archiving, it keeps no copy, so whatever was only in that staging is gone. If it holds something you want, download a backup before the deadline.

docs.title: What you see before it happens
docs.text:
You get two warnings, and the second one reaches you whatever your notification preferences are:

When What happens 14 days before A warning, and an amber Expires in N days badge on the instance 3 days before A second, critical warning; the badge turns red On the day Deleted

The badge appears next to the instance name in the project sidebar and in the instance's own header, from the first warning on.

docs.title: How to stop it
docs.text:
• Use it. Anything in the list above starts the 90 days over.
  • Press Keep on the badge in the instance header. One click, same effect.
  • Mark it as permanent — Instance detail → Settings → Never purge automatically. For the ones that should stay regardless: a QA environment nobody logs into for months is still not disposable.

Nothing is ever deleted the day the feature notices it

Each step waits for the one before it, and deletion waits at least a day after the final warning. A platform that had been down for a month comes back and warns; it cannot warn and delete in the same pass.

Pull request previews follow the same rule, on top of being deleted when their pull request closes.

Administrators can change the 90 days, or switch the whole thing off, under Settings → Instances → Staging autopurge.

docs.title: Email on staging
docs.text:
A staging never emails anybody. Whatever it sends — password resets, order confirmations, invitations — is caught by a mail server that runs alongside it and goes no further. That is what makes it safe to restore a copy of production and click around in it: the customers in that copy are real, and none of them will hear from you.

See a staging copy of production catch every email it sends: watch it in 90 seconds.

Open Instance detail → Mails to read what was caught. The list shows when each message arrived, who it was for and what it said; open one to see the HTML as the recipient would have seen it, the plain-text alternative, and what was attached.

The mailbox is temporary

The catcher keeps everything in memory. Restarting the instance — a rebuild, an update, a stop and start — empties it. If a message matters, read it before you restart.

Clear mailbox empties it on purpose, which is the way to make "now watch what this button sends" readable.

Production is the opposite: its email is real and leaves the server. There is no Mails tab there, and the SMTP relay you configure under Networking is the one that will actually deliver: see Mail relay, which covers Microsoft 365 with OAuth2 and Send test mail.

docs.title: What a staging can reach on the internet
docs.text:
A staging is a copy of production that people poke at, so what it can talk to matters. It reaches only the hostnames on its own list; everything else is refused at the network, before Odoo ever sees it. That is what stops a staging from calling a payment gateway, a tax agency or a customer's webhook while somebody is trying things out in it.

Open Instance detail → Whitelist to see and edit the list. A new staging starts with whatever its host publishes, so in the usual case there is nothing to decide. Add the hostname of any API the code under test genuinely needs — written plainly, api.example.com, with no https://, no port and no path.

It takes a rebuild

The list is part of the instance's configuration, not a live setting. Save records it and the instance shows Changes not deployed; it applies on the next Rebuild.

Emptying the list does not open the staging up — it falls back to the shared list of its host, which is what every staging used before this existed.

Production has no such list. A production instance is yours, its traffic is not filtered by the platform, and the tab is absent rather than empty.

docs.title: Odoo's website info page is blocked
docs.text:
Odoo shows anyone the list of installed apps and its exact version at /website/info (also /es/website/info and the other languages). That tells a stranger which known flaws to try, so the proxy of every host refuses it on every instance with a 403 Forbidden, before the request reaches Odoo. Your own signed-in users lose the page too: the proxy does not know who is signed in.

To let anyone open it on one instance, turn on Allow Odoo's public website info page under Instance detail → Networking and rebuild the instance. It is off for every instance, and a staging cloned from production starts with it off. While the instance is stopped or asleep, the page stays blocked.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Hosts — where instances run.
  • Backups — how to keep their data safe.

Reference page is in progress

A full per-screen reference for the Instance detail UI is coming soon.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text: Every instance keeps two kinds of log, and the panel reads both from Instance detail → Logs.

docs.title: Odoo's log is kept day by day
docs.text:
Odoo writes its log to a file on the instance's host, and that file is rotated every night into one dated file per day. You get:

  • Today (live) — the log as it is being written, refreshed every few seconds while Live is on.
  • One file per previous day, for as long as your retention window allows (60 days by default).

This is the part that matters when you notice a problem days later: the log of the day it happened is still there. It survives rebuilds — a rebuild replaces the instance's containers, and anything kept only inside a container goes with them.

docs.title: Finding the day
docs.text:
The day picker filters as you type: type 08-17 and only the matching days remain. ◀ and ▶ step one day at a time, which is the quickest way to look around an incident.

When you do not know the date, type what you are looking for in the filter box and press Enter. The panel searches every archived day on the host and tells you which ones mention it, with the number of hits, and marks them in the day picker. Click the message in the footer to jump straight to the most recent match.

Searching within a day you already have open also runs on the host, so a filter over a large day comes back with just the matching lines.

docs.title: Downloading a day
docs.text: Download hands you the selected day as a compressed file, ready to grep locally or attach to a ticket. Very large files are truncated at the platform's download cap.

docs.title: The other containers
docs.text: The database, backup and mail containers keep logging the usual way (Docker's own log, capped so they cannot fill the host's disk). Pick them in the service selector; they show their most recent output, not a per-day archive.

docs.title: Who can read logs, and what is recorded
docs.text:
Reading logs requires the Developer role or higher, and you only see instances you already have access to.

Log access is recorded in the instance's audit log (Instance detail → Audit Logs):

  • opening the log viewer for an instance,
  • searching every archived day (the search term is recorded),
  • downloading a day.

Routine refreshes of the live tail are not recorded — one entry every few seconds would bury the entries that matter.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Reading logs costs the instance's host work, so the platform bounds it. Your operator can tune all of these in Settings → Logs & retention → Instance logs and Settings → Rate limits:

Limit Default What it does Odoo log archive 60 days How many days are kept per instance Download cap 64 MB Largest download served (compressed) Search: days swept 60 How many days a cross-day search reads Search timeout 30 s When a search is cut short — it says so Log reads per user 60/min Live tail, day listing, opening a day Log searches and downloads per user 6/min The expensive ones

If a search is cut short by its timeout, the panel says so rather than reporting "no matches" — the days it had not reached yet are simply unknown, not empty.

docs.title: When something is wrong
docs.text: If the log viewer offers no days at all, the instance has not been rebuilt since per-day logs were introduced: its next rebuild starts the archive. Your operator also gets an alert if an instance stops writing to its log file or if the daily rotation stops running.

docs.title: Mail relay
docs.text:
A production instance sends its email through a mail relay: a small mail server next to Odoo that hands every message to your provider's SMTP server. Odoo always sends to the relay; what changes is how the relay signs in to your provider. You set it under Instance detail → Networking, and a rebuild applies it.

The relay signs in in one of two ways:

  • Password: a user and a password for your provider's SMTP server.
  • OAuth2 – Microsoft 365: an app registered in Microsoft Entra ID, for a mailbox in Exchange Online. Microsoft is retiring SMTP sign-in with passwords in Exchange Online, so a relay through smtp.office365.com with a password stops sending once it is off for your organisation.

A staging never uses the relay: its mail is captured on the server and shown in its Mails tab.

docs.title: OAuth2 with Microsoft 365
docs.text: The relay sends as one Microsoft 365 mailbox, the sender mailbox, through smtp.office365.com, port 587, with STARTTLS. It signs in with the client credentials of an app you register in your Microsoft 365 organisation. You need an administrator who can register apps in Entra ID and run Exchange Online PowerShell.

docs.title: 1. Register the app in Entra ID
docs.text:
1. In the Microsoft Entra admin center, open App registrations → New registration. Give it a name (for example Odoo mail relay), keep Single tenant and register it.
  2. On the app's Overview, copy the Application (client) ID and the Directory (tenant) ID.
  3. Open API permissions → Add a permission → APIs my organization uses, search for Office 365 Exchange Online, choose Application permissions and tick SMTP.SendAsApp. Then Grant admin consent.
  4. Open Certificates & secrets → New client secret. Copy its Value (not its Secret ID) at once: Entra ID shows it only now. A secret lasts at most 24 months; note when it expires.

docs.title: 2. Give the app the mailbox in Exchange Online
docs.text:
Connect with Connect-ExchangeOnline as an administrator, then:

  1. Register the app's service principal. Use the Object ID shown under Enterprise applications (search for the app's name there), not the one under App registrations: the wrong one makes the sign-in fail.

    New-ServicePrincipal -AppId <Application (client) ID> -ObjectId <Object ID from Enterprise applications>

  2. Give it the sender mailbox:

    Add-MailboxPermission -Identity notifications@example.com -User <Object ID from Enterprise applications> -AccessRights FullAccess

  3. Turn SMTP sign-in on for that mailbox. OAuth2 needs it on too:

    Set-CASMailbox -Identity notifications@example.com -SmtpClientAuthenticationDisabled $false

    If SMTP sign-in is off for the whole organisation, turn it on there as well (Set-TransportConfig -SmtpClientAuthenticationDisabled $false).

  4. Check how your organisation protects sign-ins in Entra ID. Microsoft blocks SMTP sign-in with 535 5.7.139 whatever the settings above say in one case: while Entra ID's security defaults are on.

    • With Conditional Access, security defaults are already off: allow SMTP for this app in your policies and nothing else changes.
    • With security defaults on and no Conditional Access, they have to be turned off (Entra admin center → Overview → Properties → Manage security defaults). Protect sign-ins then with Conditional Access policies, such as multifactor authentication for your users.

    The change can take a few minutes to apply.

Give the app this one mailbox only: whoever holds its secret can send as it.

docs.title: 3. Fill in the relay
docs.text:
Under Instance detail → Networking:

  1. SMTP authentication: OAuth2 – Microsoft 365. The host, port and encryption are set for you.
  2. Sender mailbox: the mailbox of step 2.
  3. Directory ID and Application (client) ID: the two IDs of step 1.
  4. Client secret: the secret's value. Once saved, it is never shown again.
  5. Save, then Rebuild the instance.

Odoo's outgoing mail must be sent as the sender mailbox. To send as another address, give the mailbox Send As on it (Add-RecipientPermission -Identity sales@example.com -Trustee notifications@example.com -AccessRights SendAs); without it Microsoft refuses the mail with 5.2.252 SendAsDenied.

The password you had is kept: switching back to Password finds it.

docs.title: Send test mail
docs.text: Under the relay's fields, Send test mail sends one mail to your own address through the relay, and the job says whether your provider's server took it, with its answer. It is available once the instance is deployed, running and its changes are applied, five times an hour. A mail that did not leave is removed from the relay's queue; one that did also sends at once the mail that was waiting. When the server only defers the mail for a reason the panel does not recognise, the job gives no verdict and the regular checks decide.

docs.title: When the relay does not deliver
docs.text:
The panel checks every production relay every few minutes. When it cannot hand mail to your provider's server for two checks in a row, counting only mail the relay has already tried again, it raises a critical alert, smtp_relay_failing, with the cause and what to do. Mail is not lost meanwhile: it waits in the relay's queue for up to 5 days and is sent as soon as the relay can; after that it goes back to its sender. A server refusing one recipient (a full or unknown mailbox) is not a relay failure and raises nothing.

The alert closes only when mail goes out again: a test mail that was sent, or any mail the relay delivers after the last failure the panel saw.

What the alert says What to do SMTP AUTH is disabled (535 5.7.139) Turn SMTP sign-in on for the mailbox and the organisation, and turn off security defaults (step 2). The server refuses the app's token (535 5.7.3) Register the service principal with the Object ID from Enterprise applications, and give it FullAccess on the mailbox (step 2). Entra ID refuses the client secret Copy the secret's Value, not its Secret ID, into the relay. The client secret has expired Create a new secret in Entra ID, save it in the relay and rebuild. Entra ID does not find the application or the directory Check both IDs on the app's Overview. The server refuses the sender (5.2.252 SendAsDenied) Send from the mailbox, or give it Send As on the other address. Microsoft no longer takes passwords Switch the relay to OAuth2 – Microsoft 365. The server refuses the connection, does not answer, or does not resolve Check the SMTP host and port, and that the server's firewall lets the instance's server out on that port. TLS fails, or the server offers no STARTTLS Check the port and the encryption. The relay's content filter (Amavis) does not take the mail Restart the instance; if it goes on, rebuild it.

Exchange Online limits how much one mailbox sends (see Microsoft's sending limits). Above them it defers the mail, which the relay sends again later.

docs.title: Memory and resources
docs.text: Instance detail → Resources sets how much memory and CPU each container of the instance may use: Odoo, the database, the backups and the mail relay. A container that reaches its memory limit has a process killed by the system, so the panel also sizes Odoo and PostgreSQL to stay inside those limits.

docs.title: What the panel sets for you
docs.text:
When you deploy or rebuild an instance, the panel derives these settings from its memory limits:

Setting From Value Odoo limit_memory_soft Odoo's memory limit 60 %, between 640 MiB and 2048 MiB Odoo limit_memory_hard Odoo's memory limit 150 %, between 1536 MiB and 2560 MiB PostgreSQL shared_buffers the database's memory limit a quarter, at least 16 MB PostgreSQL work_mem the database's memory limit a sixteenth, between 4 MB and 64 MB PostgreSQL effective_cache_size the database's memory limit half, at least 32 MB

For example, with the defaults (Odoo 2g, database 1g): each Odoo process is recycled past 1228 MiB and stopped at 2560 MiB, and PostgreSQL runs with shared_buffers = 256MB, work_mem = 64MB and effective_cache_size = 512MB. An instance with no memory limit keeps Odoo's and PostgreSQL's own defaults. The Odoo limits are set only when Odoo runs workers (workers above 0 in Config; a staging always runs three): without workers Odoo measures the soft limit on the whole server and would restart itself over and over.

Why. Odoo's own defaults (2 GiB soft and 2.5 GiB hard per worker) are more than a whole container usually has, so no worker was ever recycled: each one grew a little every day, mostly during the nightly jobs, and the instance sat near its limit until a restart. With limit_memory_soft, a worker that grows past it finishes the request it is serving and is replaced by a fresh one; you do not see it. The floors exist because Odoo measures the soft limit against a process's virtual size, which is larger than the memory it really uses, and because PDF reports run inside the hard limit. The PostgreSQL settings replace a work_mem of 512 MB, which let a single large query take more memory than the database container has.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text: On the next Deploy or Rebuild. Saving a new memory limit changes nothing on the server until then. The rebuild restarts Odoo, and the database too when its settings change: a few seconds, after which Odoo reconnects by itself.

docs.title: Using your own values
docs.text:
• Odoo: write limit_memory_soft or limit_memory_hard, in bytes, in Instance detail → Config. If either one is there, the panel sets neither and yours apply as written. 0 turns a limit off.
  • PostgreSQL: run ALTER SYSTEM SET work_mem = '128MB'; and then SELECT pg_reload_conf(); in the instance's database (shared_buffers needs a restart of the instance). It is kept in the database's own data and survives rebuilds, but not a move to another server nor a restore into another instance, which copy the database and not its server settings: set it again there. ALTER SYSTEM RESET work_mem; goes back to the panel's value.

docs.title: Alerts about memory
docs.text:
• High memory: Odoo's container above 95 % of its limit for 30 minutes.
  • Workers recycled for memory: more than 12 Odoo workers replaced in an hour for passing limit_memory_soft. The instance works, but its workers reach the limit as soon as they warm up and requests often land on a fresh one: raise Odoo's memory limit in Resources, or set a higher limit_memory_soft in Config.
  • Out of memory: the system killed a process in the Odoo, database or mail container for lack of memory. This one is critical: something was stopped mid-way. Raise the container's limit in Resources, or look for the operation that needed that much.

The database has no alert by percentage: most of what it uses is cache, which is released when needed, so it always reads close to its limit.

See Monitoring for where alerts arrive.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text: Move an existing Odoo into IncubaCloud without rebuilding from scratch. Every move follows the same plan: bring the project, bring the data, try it while the old Odoo keeps working, and switch over at a quiet moment.

docs.title: Pick your starting point
docs.text:
• Coming from Odoo.sh — your project lives in a Git repo on Odoo.sh and you can download backups from the dashboard. Walkthrough

  • Coming from another host — your own server, a hosting provider, Docker or a package install: what to check first, the three ways to bring the project, the data, a test, and the switch. Walkthrough

  • Importing an instance already running on a VPS — doodba already deployed on a host you can SSH into, and you want to bring it under IncubaCloud's management without redeploying. Use Host detail → Import Instance in the SPA. We read .copier-answers.yml, repos.yaml, addons.yaml, .env and the docker-compose file directly.

  • Importing a project from Git — your custom code is in a Git repo (doodba layout via .copier-answers.yml or Odoo.sh layout via .gitmodules) and you'll restore data later via the Backups → Restore flow. Use Dashboard → New Project and paste the repo URL.

docs.title: What we cannot do (yet)
docs.text:
• Live sync — we don't replicate continuously from a running instance.
  • Detection from a *.odoo.sh URL — you must paste the Git URL of the repo, not the Odoo.sh dashboard URL.
  • Cutover with zero downtime — the instance is briefly unavailable during the database restore.
  • Automatic neutralization of restored DBs — restored databases keep their original cron jobs, mail servers, and admin users. To neutralize, download the neutralized backup instead and import that.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Backups → Restore — the second half of any data migration.
  • Hosts → Connect — needed if your data lives on a VPS we don't manage yet.

docs.title: Migrate from another host
docs.text: Your company's Odoo runs somewhere else today: on a server of your own, at a hosting provider, in Docker or installed as a package. This page moves it to IncubaCloud with what the panel already does: import the project, bring the data, try it, and switch over. For Odoo.sh, see Migrate from Odoo.sh, which follows the same plan.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Write down four things about the Odoo you have:

What Where to find it Why Odoo version In Odoo, Settings, at the bottom (for example Odoo 18.0) The new instance runs the same one: a restore does not change versions. Edition Settings: Community or Enterprise Enterprise needs its code and your own Odoo Enterprise subscription (Projects). Your own modules In Odoo, Apps, filter Installed: those that are neither Odoo's nor in its app store, or ask whoever wrote them Their code has to be in a Git repository the project reads. Size of the data The size of a backup ZIP It decides how the file reaches the panel.

Same version, or upgrade first

The panel does not upgrade a database to another Odoo version. To move to a newer version, upgrade the database first, with Odoo's upgrade service for Enterprise or with OpenUpgrade for Community, and restore the upgraded one.

Odoo Online

A database on Odoo Online runs Odoo Enterprise, sometimes on an intermediate version only Odoo hosts. Before you download its backup, have it on a major version (such as 18.0 or 19.0), and plan for the Enterprise subscription, or for leaving the Enterprise apps behind.

docs.title: 1. Get a host and backups
docs.text: If you have not yet: a host of the right size (which one) and a backup destination. A production instance is not deployed without the second.

docs.title: 2. Bring the project
docs.text:
Pick the case that matches where your Odoo runs.

A doodba project on a serverCode in a Git repositoryNo code of your own

Your Odoo runs from a doodba project folder (with .copier-answers.yml) on a server you reach by SSH.

  1. Connect that server to the panel, as a host.
  2. Open it in Hosts, then More → Import Instance.
  3. Browse to the project's folder and import it.

The panel reads the project's files (.copier-answers.yml, repos.yaml, addons.yaml, the .env files and the Compose override) and creates the project and its instance as they are, without deploying again. You can skip steps 3 and 4: the data is already there.

Your own modules are in a Git repository: a doodba project, an Odoo.sh one, or one with modules only.

  1. On Projects, press Import from GitHub and paste the repository's URL (for GitLab, see Repositories on GitLab).
  2. Pick the branch. The panel reads the Odoo version and the repositories from it, and creates the project with a production instance ready to deploy.

A private repository needs the panel's GitHub App or a token first: Create your first project.

Your Odoo uses only Odoo's modules, and perhaps some from the app store.

  1. On Projects, press New Project, and choose the Odoo version of your database.
  2. Add the production instance with the same modules, as in Deploy your first instance.

Modules from the app store go in a Git repository of yours, for the project to read them.

docs.title: 3. Deploy the production instance
docs.text: Deploy it once, empty: it is what the data is restored into. Choose on its Database tab a PostgreSQL of the same major version as today's, or a newer one.

docs.title: 4. Bring the data
docs.text:
Make a ZIP of the database with its filestore on the old host, and restore it on the new instance with Restore Database.

Two Odoos sending the same mail

Nothing is switched off by the restore: the new production comes back with the scheduled actions and the mail servers of the old one. While the old Odoo runs, both would send the same mail to your customers and fetch the same mailboxes. Switch them off on the new one right after restoring (point 3).

  1. Make the ZIP: from Odoo's database manager (/web/database/manager, Backup, format zip), or by hand on the server. The steps for both.
  2. Send it the way its size allows: through your browser (up to 2 GB by default), through SSH with a temporary upload key (no limit), or as a link the host downloads itself (no limit): Restore from an external ZIP.
  3. Right after it, switch off in the new Odoo, with the developer mode on, under Settings → Technical: the Automation → Scheduled Actions, and the Email → Outgoing Mail Servers and Email → Incoming Mail Servers. Select them all and archive them (Actions → Archive). The final restore of step 6 brings them back.
  4. Sign in with the users and passwords of the old database.

docs.title: 5. Try it before you switch
docs.text:
The old Odoo keeps working while you try the new one: nobody has moved yet.

  • Try it in a staging, not in production. Clone to Staging makes a copy where mail goes nowhere (why), so you can open documents and run your usual tasks without writing to your customers.
  • Check what matters to you: the last invoices, stock, reports, your own modules' screens, an import you do every week.
  • Keep the scheduled actions and mail servers off on the new production until the switch (step 4, details).

docs.title: 6. Switch over
docs.text:
Pick a quiet moment, outside working hours, and tell your team.

  1. The day before, lower the TTL of your domain's DNS record, if your DNS lets you, to a few minutes: the change will then be seen sooner.
  2. Stop work on the old Odoo: stop it, or tell everyone not to use it.
  3. Make a fresh ZIP and restore it on the new production (step 4), so nothing done since the test is lost. This time leave the scheduled actions and the mail servers on: the old Odoo no longer runs.
  4. Point your domain at the new host: change the A record to the new host's IP address, and add the name to the instance's Networking → Domains (how).
  5. Deploy the instance for its certificate, sign in, and check that mail leaves (outgoing mail).

Keep the old host as it is for a few days, stopped, in case you need to look something up. Cancel it when you are sure.

docs.title: Verify it worked
docs.text:
• Your domain opens the new instance, with HTTPS.
  • The last documents from before the switch are there.
  • A test mail arrived, and not in spam.
  • The morning after, the instance's Backups tab lists a backup.

docs.title: If you need help
docs.text:
Open an issue on GitHub with where your Odoo runs today, its version and edition, the size of a backup, and whether it has modules of your own.

IncubaCloud SaaS

Write to us through the contact form with the same details. We reply with the steps for your case.

docs.title: Migrate from Odoo.sh
docs.text:
Two steps: import the project from your Git repo, then restore the database from the backup ZIP you download from Odoo.sh. Each step is straightforward.

Honest expectation

A full Odoo.sh migration is two steps, not one click. We don't do live sync. We don't promise zero downtime during cutover. Restore time depends on dump size — budget 10–30 minutes for a typical customer database.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Your project's Git URL (find it on the Odoo.sh dashboard).
  • A backup ZIP from Odoo.sh.
  • An IncubaCloud account — for production use a paid plan (on Free your control plane sleeps when idle and gets no automatic backups).
  • A host (yours or hired).

docs.title: Step 1 — import the project from Git
docs.text:
1. On the Odoo.sh dashboard, copy your project's GitHub URL. The plain HTTPS form (https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>) and the SSH form (git@github.com:<owner>/<repo>.git) both work.
  2. In IncubaCloud, on Projects, click Import from GitHub. Paste the URL and pick the branch.
  3. We auto-detect the Odoo.sh layout via .gitmodules and reconstruct the project structure: submodules, branches, Odoo version (from the project's requirements.txt or pinned image).
  4. Click Import. The project shows up with the detected branches and version pre-filled, and with a production instance ready to deploy. Versions 8.0 to 20.0 are recognized; a project on another one, or whose version cannot be read, is imported on the newest version the panel offers.

Private repos need credentials

Connect the platform's GitHub App, or store a personal access token, in Settings → GitHub before importing. A URL with a token inside it (https://<token>@github.com/...) is refused: credentials never travel in the URL. There are no deploy keys; access goes through the App or the token.

docs.title: Step 2 — restore the database
docs.text:
1. Download a backup from Odoo.sh. From the project's Backups tab, pick the most recent ZIP. The format is the standard Odoo dump (dump.sql + filestore/).
  2. In IncubaCloud, deploy the production instance the import created, with the same Odoo version. Don't worry about the data — you're about to overwrite it.
  3. Open the instance → Restore Database.
  4. Send the ZIP through your browser, and for a large database use the temporary upload key or paste a link to it instead (see the restore docs).
  5. The restore job runs and replaces the empty database with your real one.

docs.title: Step 3 — cut over
docs.text:
Point your DNS to the IncubaCloud instance:

A    app.example.com    →    <new host IP>

DNS propagation usually takes a few minutes. Once it's through, your customers land on the new instance. Old Odoo.sh instance can stay running until you're confident, then cancel.

Restored DB is not neutralized

Your restored database keeps the original cron jobs, mail servers, and admin users. If you restore to a staging instance for testing, disable mail and crons before running scenarios that send emails or trigger automations. Or: use the neutralized backup download on the Odoo.sh side first and import that.

docs.title: Verify it worked
docs.text:
• You can log in to the restored instance with the original admin credentials.
  • The data matches what you had on Odoo.sh at the time of the dump.
  • Your custom modules from the imported repo are installed and visible.
  • DNS resolves to the IncubaCloud instance with HTTPS.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Project import failed: \"layout not detected\"

We expect either .copier-answers.yml (doodba) or .gitmodules (Odoo.sh) in the repo root. Older Odoo.sh projects sometimes lack .gitmodules in the default branch. Check the branch you're importing has it.

Restore is slow

Most of the time is spent unzipping the filestore. Large filestores (10+ GB) can take an hour. Do the migration during a maintenance window.

Custom modules from Odoo.sh not loading

Odoo.sh sometimes pulls modules via submodules from private repos. Check Project → Settings → Repository and ensure the deploy key has access to all submodule repos, not just the main one.

I want to keep both running for a few days

Don't change DNS yet. Test the IncubaCloud instance via its auto-generated subdomain. When confident, flip DNS in your registrar.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text: A project groups everything that belongs to one customer or one product: its instances, its repositories, its environments.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
• Project — top-level container. Owned by your account.
  • Environment — production or staging. Each project has one production and any number of stagings.
  • Repository — Git URL where your custom modules live, on GitHub or on GitLab. Detected as doodba (via .copier-answers.yml) or Odoo.sh (via .gitmodules).
  • Backup backend — the S3 destination for backups. Inherited from project unless overridden per instance.

Odoo Enterprise

A project can deploy Odoo Community or Odoo Enterprise. The panel itself runs on Community only, and IncubaCloud does not provide Enterprise: for an Enterprise instance, you bring its code in your repositories and need your own Odoo Enterprise subscription ("On-premise") from Odoo S.A. See Third-party software.

docs.title: Repositories
docs.text: A project's repositories are GitHub repositories, written https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>; other spellings of a GitHub address are rewritten to that form, and any other host is refused. The project's list is copied to each instance created in it; an instance's own list is the one its deploys use.

docs.title: Private repositories
docs.text:
The panel reads a private repository with credentials from Settings → GitHub: the GitHub App, or a Personal Access Token, which also reaches repositories the App cannot (odoo/enterprise, for instance). A token written inside the repository's URL is refused.

Only the App receives GitHub's push and pull request notifications, which Auto-rebuild and pull request previews need, and only on a panel GitHub can reach from the internet. A token gives access, with manual deploys and rebuilds.

docs.title: Which modules a repository brings
docs.text:
Each repository row has Modules and Exclude:

  • Modules empty — shown as ALL — makes every module of the repository available to the instance.
  • Modules with names makes only those available: the list replaces ALL, it does not add to it.
  • Exclude takes modules out of ALL. It only has a meaning while Modules is empty.

Available is not installed. The first deploy installs base and the panel's sign-in module only; you install the rest from Odoo's Apps, or they come installed with a database you restore.

auto_install modules and ALL

Odoo installs a module marked auto_install by itself once every module it depends on is installed — at the first deploy, or later when you install something from Apps. With ALL, every such module of the repository is available, so it is installed as soon as its dependencies are, whether you wanted it or not. To keep one out, list the modules you want instead, or put it under Exclude.

Two repositories that bring a module of the same name stop the deploy with a conflict alert; Exclude in one of them is the usual way out.

docs.title: Freezing a repository
docs.text:
Freeze (the lock on a repository row, or Freeze all) pins the repository to the commit its branch points to at that moment:

  • every deploy and rebuild builds that commit, not the branch's newest one;
  • a push to the branch does not rebuild the instance;
  • the repository's requirements.txt is not read again.

Unfreeze to follow the branch again.

docs.title: Python and system packages
docs.text:
• A repository's own requirements.txt is read on every deploy and rebuild (frozen repositories excepted), and what it lists is installed.
  • The Dependencies tab — of the project, as the default for new instances, or of an instance — has pip.txt — Python and apt.txt — System: one package per line, installed in the instance's image at the next deploy or rebuild. Sync with project, on an instance, brings the project's lists over.

A package listed in a requirements.txt and in the Dependencies tab with different versions stops the build with a dependency conflict alert: open it and pick which one wins.

docs.title: Repositories on GitLab
docs.text: A project can deploy and rebuild from GitLab repositories, on gitlab.com or on a GitLab server of your own, alone or mixed with GitHub repositories in the same project.

docs.title: Add the server
docs.text:
Settings → Git providers → Add a GitLab server.

  • Base URL: https://gitlab.com, or your server's address. https only; add the port or the path prefix if your server has one (https://git.example.com:8443/gitlab).
  • CA certificate: only when a private CA signs your server's certificate. Paste the CA's certificate (PEM); the panel shows its SHA-256 fingerprint so you can check it. The panel never turns certificate checks off.
  • Credentials: one token per namespace. The namespace is empty for the whole server, or a group, a subgroup or a project path (acme, acme/odoo, acme/odoo/addons). A repository uses the token of the longest namespace that covers it. A repository no token covers is read as a public one.

The token is stored encrypted and never shown again; leave the field empty to keep it. It only travels to its own server: in a project that mixes GitLab and GitHub, each repository is cloned with its own credential.

Test connection, with the URL of one of your repositories, checks two things and says what failed in each:

  • git: the panel can read the repository with its credential;
  • API: the token answers on GitLab's API, with its scopes and expiry.

The panel has to reach the GitLab server over the network. A panel limited to public addresses refuses a server with a private one.

docs.title: Which token
docs.text:
What the panel does Scope Token types Deploy, rebuild, list branches and modules, pin a commit, the assistant's reads read_repository (Reporter role) deploy token, project, group or personal token Show a token's scopes and expiry any scope project, group or personal token Register the webhook api (Maintainer role; Owner for a group) project, group or personal token Write the preview's note on a merge request api project, group or personal token
  • To deploy, a deploy token or a project access token with read_repository, one per repository, is enough. A deploy token needs its own user name (gitlab+deploy-token-N) and does not answer on GitLab's API, so the panel shows it as no API; set its expiry by hand if it has one.
  • Project, group and personal tokens expire (one year at most by default). The panel warns two weeks before a token it knows the expiry of runs out.
  • On gitlab.com Free there are no project or group tokens: use a deploy token, or a personal token of a bot user.

docs.title: Repository URLs
docs.text:
Type the repository's address in the project's or the instance's repository list, as https://gitlab.com/acme/addons, gitlab.com/acme/addons or git@gitlab.com:acme/addons.git. The panel stores it as https://gitlab.com/acme/addons.git: GitLab answers an address without .git with a redirect, and the panel follows no redirects. A line shows its server as GitLab · gitlab.com.

An address of a server that is not under Settings → Git providers is refused, naming the server. Importing an instance from a host leaves such repositories out and lists them: add the server and import again.

docs.title: Odoo 8.0 to 10.0
docs.text: The images of these series carry a git too old to be trusted with a token. For them the panel downloads every repository of the instance before the build, with git of its own, and the image's git touches none: no token reaches the image. A repository whose address redirects (a moved project) fails: correct its address.

docs.title: Rebuild on push: webhooks
docs.text:
A GitLab repository rebuilds its instances on every push through a webhook of the panel. After you save GitLab lines, the repository editor shows the state of each one's webhook:

  • Register webhook: with a credential that has the api scope and the Maintainer role in the project (Owner for a group), the panel creates the webhook in GitLab itself, with push and merge request events and SSL verification. Without that role, it says why and you set it up by hand.
  • Set up by hand: a manager sees the URL and the secret under Settings → Git providers → Webhooks. In GitLab, open Settings → Webhooks → Add new webhook, paste both, tick Push events and Merge request events, keep Enable SSL verification and save. Then press Test → Tag push events: never Push events, which repeats your last push and rebuilds.
  • A manager can register one webhook for a whole group, on GitLab tiers that have group webhooks: it covers every project below the group.

Verify asks GitLab for a test delivery (a tag push, which rebuilds nothing) and the list shows when it arrived. GitLab allows five tests a minute per webhook, so the panel waits 15 seconds between two.

GitLab never resends a delivery on its own: one that failed is lost, and on gitlab.com four failures in a row disable the webhook for a while (forty, for good). The panel checks every day and warns you when GitLab disabled it; press Verify to enable it again, and rebuild by hand the instances that missed a push. On a GitLab server of your own this switch is off unless its administrator turned on auto_disabling_web_hooks.

The same delivery sent twice (GitLab's Resend) or the same push twice does not rebuild twice: press Rebuild if you want another build.

Webhooks that arrive while the panel is stopped (GitLab's and GitHub's) are lost: rebuild by hand after a push.

docs.title: Merge request previews
docs.text:
With Preview instances for pull requests and merge requests on in the project's settings, a merge request gets a preview as a GitHub pull request does (see Pull request previews): a staging named mr-<number> on the production's host, with the merge request's branch and a neutralized copy of the production's data. It needs the repository's webhook, with Merge request events.

  • Opening or reopening the merge request creates the preview, from each production instance whose own repository lines follow the project, unpinned. The project's lines, a template for new instances, do not count.
  • New commits on its branch rebuild it. Editing the title, the labels or the reviewers, and approvals, do nothing.
  • Closing or merging it deletes the preview, also while it is still being created: the panel waits for the step running then.
  • Once the preview is up, the panel writes a note on the merge request with its address, and takes it off when the merge request closes. The note needs a credential of the repository with the api scope; without one the preview works without its note. If GitLab does not answer, the panel tries again for about 20 minutes; then, or at once if GitLab refuses the note, an alert says the note could not be written: on the preview for its address, on the production instance for a note saying why no preview was created. The next note that goes through resolves it, and so does closing the merge request.
  • A merge request from a fork gets no preview: a preview runs the branch with a copy of production's data, so only branches of the project itself count. The panel says so in a note on the merge request.
  • If a preview cannot be created, the merge request gets a note saying why and the production instance an alert. Fix the cause, then close and reopen the merge request.

docs.title: What the panel does not do with GitLab
docs.text:
• Importing a project from Odoo.sh reads GitHub only: Odoo.sh works with GitHub.
  • The assistant reads GitLab repositories but does not write to them yet: branches, commits and merge requests come in a next version.

IncubaCloud SaaS

This page describes the hosted service at incubacloud.io. A panel you install yourself sits behind whatever you put in front of it, so none of these numbers apply to it.

Instances on the hosted service are served through a CDN. That buys you TLS, caching and protection against floods, and it comes with two limits that you can run into from inside your own Odoo.

docs.title: One request may carry at most 100 MB
docs.text:
A single HTTP request cannot carry more than 100 MB of body. Past that the CDN answers 413 Request Entity Too Large and your Odoo never sees the upload.

In practice this bites when you attach a very large file, or import one, from the Odoo web client.

What to do instead

You are… Use Restoring a database dump Restore a backup — the browser route sends the file in pieces, so the 100 MB ceiling does not apply. For very large dumps, the SSH or link routes bypass the CDN entirely. Attaching a large document Store it in object storage and attach the link, or split the file. Importing a large data file Split the import into several files.

docs.title: One request may take at most 100 seconds
docs.text:
The CDN waits 100 seconds for your instance to start answering. If a request takes longer to produce its first byte, the CDN gives up and returns 524 A timeout occurred — even though your Odoo usually keeps working and finishes the job in the background.

This is a limit on a single request, not on the work itself. It shows up on things like a report over a very large date range, a heavy import run synchronously, or a query with no index behind it.

What to do instead

  • Narrow the range or the batch, and run the operation in several passes.
  • Prefer Odoo's scheduled actions for long jobs: they run server-side with no request waiting on them.
  • If an operation you need genuinely cannot finish in 100 seconds, tell us — that is usually a sign the operation should be moved to a background job.

A 524 does not mean the work was lost

The request was abandoned, not the job. Reload the page before repeating the operation: quite often it completed.

docs.title: Where managed backups are stored
docs.text:
If you use Managed Backup Storage (the paid add-on that provisions a bucket for you instead of you bringing your own), the bucket lives on Cloudflare R2 in the European Union — the endpoint is eu.r2.cloudflarestorage.com, and the data does not leave that jurisdiction.

Backups are encrypted with your passphrase before they leave the host, so the storage provider holds ciphertext only. See Backups.

If you bring your own bucket, backups live wherever your bucket lives and this does not apply.

docs.title: Third parties in the path
docs.text:
Traffic to instances on the hosted service is proxied by Cloudflare, which therefore processes connection metadata (source address, hostname, request headers) on our behalf. Cloudflare also stores managed backup buckets, as described above.

For the contractual side — the full list of the providers we rely on, and the data-protection terms that govern them — see the privacy policy and the terms of service.
