docs.title: Monitoring panels
docs.text:
What each chart shows, what a healthy one looks like, and what to do when it looks wrong. For what is measured and how to switch it on, see Monitoring.

Charts refresh every minute and open on the last 6 hours. Use the time picker to change that: 1h while watching a deploy, 7d to tell a spike from a trend.

Alerts do the watching for you

Where a card says this is alerted, you need not keep the page open: the rule is checked every five minutes and reaches you through your notification channels. Cards without that note are yours to read.

docs.title: Fleet
docs.text:
Open Monitoring in the sidebar. This tab answers "is anything wrong anywhere?" and needs no selection — every host you manage is on it.

The top row reads left to right: three cards about your hosts, then two about your instances.

Card What it shows Healthy Hosts reporting How many hosts sent a sample in the last five minutes The number of hosts you manage Hosts above 90% disk Count of hosts whose root disk is nearly full 0 Hosts above 92% memory Count of hosts nearly out of memory 0 Instances deployed How many instances are installed on your hosts, awake or asleep Your instance count Instances running How many instances have Odoo up right now Your instance count, minus any that are asleep

Load per core, by host. The 15-minute load average divided by the number of cores, top ten hosts. A ratio, not a percentage: 1 means the host is using exactly the CPU it has. Below 1 is comfortable, sustained above 2 is a host that cannot keep up — this is alerted. Brief peaks during a deploy or a backup are normal.

Root filesystem used % and Memory used %, by host. Top ten hosts, as percentages. Disk is the one to act on early: it does not recover on its own, and a full disk stops an instance dead. Alerted at 90% and 92% respectively.

Ingest age per host. One lane per host, green while it is reporting and red once it has been silent for more than five minutes. Unbroken green is what you want; a lane turning red means the machine is down, or just its agent. This is alerted.

Why a lane per host and not lines

Every agent samples on the same clock tick, so on a shared axis the hosts drew identical lines on top of each other and all but one were invisible. Lanes cannot hide each other, and the colour change sits on the alert's own threshold — chart and alert can never disagree.

docs.title: Hosts
docs.text:
One host at a time. Pick it with the Host selector above the charts — it starts on your first host, so check the selector before reading the numbers.

CPU load per core. The same ratio as the fleet card, for this host alone. Around or below 1 is healthy; sustained above 2 is alerted.

Memory used % and Root filesystem used %. This host's totals. Alerted at 92% and 90% respectively.

Disk used per instance. Disk taken by each instance on this host, in bytes. When the disk percentage climbs, this is the card that names the culprit — usually a database that has grown or backups piling up locally, see Backups. There is no per-instance alert (a byte threshold means nothing across instances of very different sizes); the host disk alert is what warns you.

HTTP requests by Traefik service (requests per second) and Request duration p95 by Traefik service (seconds). Traffic through this host's proxy, grouped by service. p95 means 95% of requests finished faster than the line shows; watch its shape, not its absolute value, since a heavy report is legitimately slow. A p95 climbing while requests stay flat is the interesting one: the same load is getting harder to serve.

Why by service and not by instance

The proxy reports per service, and service names come from each deployment's own configuration, so they cannot be attributed back to a single instance. For one instance's traffic, use its Metrics tab instead.

docs.title: Instances
docs.text:
One instance at a time, with a Host selector and an Instance selector. Set the host first: container names repeat across machines, and without the host two instances with the same container name would be added together.

CPU per container. One line per container of the instance, in cores. A container at 1.0 is using a full core. The Odoo container doing the work while the others idle is the normal shape.

Memory per container. Working set per container, in bytes. A slow, permanent climb in the Odoo container between restarts is worth investigating; a database container that settles on a plateau is doing its job.

Neither card is alerted on its own. What is alerted is the instance going quiet altogether: no container reporting for five minutes.

IncubaCloud SaaS

An instance on a plan that sleeps when idle stops its containers on purpose. It disappears from these charts while asleep and does not raise an alert for it.

docs.title: An instance's Metrics tab
docs.text: Open an instance and go to Metrics. The tab is a diagnosis of that instance, already pinned to it and to its host: nothing to select. It reads top to bottom as the questions you ask when an instance is slow.

docs.title: What is happening now?
docs.text:
A card with a coloured edge — green, amber or red — and a few sentences about the last 15 minutes: which resource is short and what to do about it. The sentences come from fixed rules over the charts below, with these thresholds:

The card says When Odoo is held back by its CPU quota Odoo was refused CPU by its quota more than 25% of the time The server is saturated and most of it goes to another instance The server's load is above 2 per core and another instance uses more than half of the server's CPU Memory is short The server's tasks waited for memory more than 10% of the time, or the kernel killed a process of this instance for lack of memory, in the last 15 minutes The server's disk is the bottleneck The server's tasks waited for the disk more than 20% of the time Requests take long without using CPU or the database The proxy's p95 is above 2 seconds while Odoo and the database each use less than 30% of a core: usually a call to an outside service Odoo restarted N minutes ago Odoo's container started in the last 15 minutes No resource looks saturated None of the above

Zoomed into the past, the card does not judge: it only reads the last 15 minutes up to now. The buttons under it take you to Queries now, Slow routes and Recent requests.

docs.title: Since when?
docs.text:
Request time (p50 and p95) and Requests (per second, with server errors in red), measured at the proxy for this instance alone. Choose 1h, 6h, 24h or 7d (it opens on 1h); drag across any chart, with the mouse or a finger moving sideways, to zoom every chart into that window, and Reset zoom to go back. 1h and 6h refresh every 45 seconds while the tab is open.

Two marks run over the charts: a blue dot (●) where a container restarted and a red triangle (▲) where the kernel killed one of its processes for lack of memory.

docs.title: Which resource?
docs.text:
CPU per container. One line per container, 100% being one core; the dashed line of the same colour is the container's CPU quota (Resources). Odoo doing the work while the others idle is the normal shape.

Held back by the CPU quota. The share of time each container wanted CPU and its quota said no. A few percent is normal; Odoo above 25% for long means its requests queue behind the quota.

Memory per container. Working set per container, with its limit dashed. A slow, permanent climb in the Odoo container between restarts is worth investigating; a database that settles on a plateau is doing its job. On the 7-day range each point is the highest value of its interval, so short peaks still show.

Server: waiting for resources. The share of time some task of the whole server waited for CPU, memory or the disk (the kernel's pressure figures). Near zero is healthy. It tells a server that is short of something apart from an instance that is merely busy.

Neighbours. CPU of every instance on the same server, this one in green. When the server is saturated, this card says whether this instance is the cause or another one is.

docs.title: Which process or query?
docs.text:
A line with the Odoo workers configured and an estimate of how busy they are (Odoo's CPU over the last 15 minutes against one core per worker). Then two readings taken from the host only when you press their button; one runs at a time, and nothing of them is stored.

Queries now reads the instance's database: how many connections it has against its maximum, how many are active, waiting on a lock or idle inside a transaction, the longest of each, the cache hit ratio and the size. Then its sessions — state, what they wait for, for how long, which program, who blocks whom (a blocked row is tinted) and the start of their query — and the ten tables with most dead rows with their last vacuum. A session idle in a transaction that blocks others is the usual culprit behind a stuck import or cron. Query texts can contain your users' data, which is why they are read on demand and only by the developer role or above.

Slow routes reads Odoo's own log for the last 15 or 60 minutes: the ten routes that took the most time in total, with their count, mean, p95, the share spent in SQL and in Python and the mean number of queries; the scheduled actions with their longest and total run, and those still running; the requests stopped by a time limit; and how many workers were recycled for memory. Where a stopped request was depends on how Odoo runs: without workers, Odoo logs its stack, and the reading shows the URL it served and its innermost calls; with workers, Odoo kills the worker without logging where it was, so there is only the time and the limit. A route with a high SQL share points at the database; a high Python share at the code. Odoo before 11.0 logs no timing: its requests are counted, not timed.

docs.title: Size
docs.text: The size of the instance's directory on the server, measured every 10 minutes.

docs.title: Recent requests
docs.text:
Below the board, read live from the host's proxy each time you press Refresh, and never stored. Five summaries over the requests read — Status codes, Top clients, Top paths, Login attempts (posts to the login page by client address) and Scanners (addresses asking for other software's files, such as WordPress pages, .env or .git, and getting a 404) — a bar of requests per minute, with the minutes that had server errors in red, then the requests themselves with time, client address, method, path and status.

This is the half the charts cannot give you: they say an instance is busy or failing, only this says what is being done to it. During an incident, read it in this order:

  1. Status codes — a wall of 5xx is the instance failing, not the load. A burst of server errors is alerted.
  2. Top clients and Login attempts — one address dominating is a scraper, a runaway integration or somebody trying passwords, not your users.
  3. Top paths — the endpoint under pressure, which is usually enough to name the cause.

If the card says no requests were recorded and you expect traffic, the host's proxy has not been redeployed since access logging was switched on.

docs.title: What you will not find here
docs.text: Database figures over time (connections, locks, cache hit ratio as charts and alerts): today they are read on demand with Queries now.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: Every host you manage reports its own health and that of the instances on it. There is nothing to install: once observability is switched on, hosts enrol themselves, and any host that fails to is retried automatically until it succeeds.

docs.title: What is measured
docs.text:
Per host — CPU, memory, disk usage and free space, load, and whether the host is reporting at all.

Per instance — CPU and memory of each container with their limits, how often the CPU quota held it back, restarts and processes killed for lack of memory, disk used by the instance's directory, and its HTTP traffic: requests per second, server errors and latency.

On demand — when you ask, from the instance's Metrics tab: what its database is doing (sessions, locks, connections) and where Odoo's time went (slowest routes, scheduled actions, workers stopped by a limit), read from the host and never stored.

Per request — the proxy also records who asked for what. That is what the Recent requests panel on an instance shows: client IP, method, path and response code. Metrics tell you an instance is under load; only these tell you what is being done to it.

docs.title: Where to look
docs.text:
One instance in trouble → open it and go to the Metrics tab. This is the right place during an incident: it says in plain words which resource is short, shows since when, compares the instance with its neighbours on the same server, reads on demand what its database and its Odoo log are doing, and underneath lists the requests hitting it right now.

The whole fleet → the Monitoring entry in the sidebar, next to Hosts. It appears only when observability is enabled.

For what each individual chart means, what a healthy one looks like and what to check when it does not, see Monitoring panels.

Is a host being monitored? → its page states it plainly: reporting, agents installed but no data yet, install failed and retrying, or not enrolled yet.

Both views need the developer role or above.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
Rules are data, not code: thresholds can be tuned without a release. Shipped rules cover a host that stopped reporting, a disk almost full, memory nearly exhausted, sustained CPU saturation, an instance that stopped reporting containers, an instance returning server errors, and a process of an instance's Odoo, database or mail container killed for lack of memory. The last one is critical.

Each instance is also checked every five minutes: its Odoo above 95 % of its memory limit for thirty minutes raises a warning, and so do more than twelve Odoo workers recycled for memory in an hour. See Memory and resources for what the panel sets so that Odoo stays below its limit.

Alerts arrive through the same channels as everything else — in-app, email, Telegram or webhook, as configured.

An instance whose plan puts it to sleep on idle does not raise a "stopped reporting" alert. Sleeping stops its containers on purpose, and alerting on it every night would train everyone to ignore the alert that matters.

docs.title: What you need for it to work
docs.text:
On IncubaCloud's SaaS — nothing. Metrics are configured for you when your panel is created, and hosts you add later are enrolled on their own.

Self-hosted — one decision: which of your hosts runs the central stack. Settings → Monitoring, pick the host, press Enable observability. The endpoints and credentials are filled in for you.

If you have hosts other than the one running the central, they need a public HTTPS address to push to; set it under Advanced. The local address the button fills in is only reachable from the central's own host. Or give the central a direct name and its host a direct port: your hosts then push to it without a CDN in between, on a port only they may open.

docs.title: What is not here
docs.text: Database figures per instance over time (connections, cache hit ratio, locks) are not charted or alerted: Queries now on the Metrics tab reads them when you ask. There are no synthetic probes from outside.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text: Stay on top of what your platform is doing without watching the screen. Every user configures their own channels from the bell menu in the header (Notifications modal).

docs.title: What triggers a notification
docs.text:
Job outcomes — a deploy, rebuild, backup or any other operation finishing (successfully or not) — and alerts. Alerts come in two levels: critical (host unreachable, instance down, disk critical…) and warning (a container of an instance down, errors in an instance's log, a declined subscription payment…). Failed deploys and rebuilds are treated as severe and always delivered immediately.

An open warning that turns critical is announced again, on every channel, to everyone whose level covers critical alerts.

docs.title: Your preferences
docs.text:
• Level — decides both which job outcomes and which alerts reach you:

    Level Jobs Alerts All every outcome critical and warning Failures and warnings (default) failed only critical and warning Failures only failed only critical only None none none

    The daily digest follows the same level. An account created before version 1.0.193 keeps the level it had (Failures only was the default). - Muted projects — silence everything from projects you don't care about. - Notifications only cover what you can already see: project visibility rules apply to every channel.

docs.title: In-app (always on)
docs.text: Toasts for finished jobs and critical alerts, plus the alert badge in the header. Real-time — no configuration needed.

docs.title: Email
docs.text:
Toggle it on and pick a mode:

  • Immediate — one email per job outcome or alert.
  • Daily digest — a single summary email every morning. Severe failures (deploy/rebuild) and critical alerts still arrive immediately.

docs.title: Telegram
docs.text:
1. Create a bot with @BotFather and paste the bot token.
  2. Send any message to your bot, then click Detect chat ID — the platform finds your chat automatically.
  3. Send test to verify. Done: job outcomes and alerts arrive as Telegram messages, following your level.

docs.title: Webhook
docs.text:
Point the platform at any HTTPS endpoint to integrate with Slack bridges, on-call tools or your own automation. Two event types arrive as JSON POSTs — job_state_change for successful job completions, and alert for failures and infrastructure alerts:

{
  "event": "job_state_change",
  "job_id": 123,
  "job_name": "Deploy Instance",
  "state": "done",
  "severe": false,
  "host": "host-1",
  "instance": "production",
  "log_url": "https://…/cloud/log/123",
  "timestamp": "2026-07-12 10:00:00"
}

{
  "event": "alert",
  "alert_id": 45,
  "code": "job_failed",
  "level": "critical",
  "message": "Deploy Instance on production failed",
  "host": "host-1",
  "instance": "production",
  "job_id": 123,
  "log_url": "https://…/cloud/log/123",
  "timestamp": "2026-07-12 10:00:00"
}

When an alert clears automatically (the monitor that raised it observes recovery), the same payload shape is sent again with "event": "alert_resolved" — consumers can close the incident they opened on the alert event. Dismissing an alert by hand in the panel does not send this event: the operator silencing it is already looking at it.

If you set a secret, every request carries an X-IncubaCloud-Signature: sha256=<hex> header — the HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body. Verify it with a constant-time comparison before trusting the payload.

docs.title: Backup usage alerts
docs.text: Separately from these notifications, each backup backend can email a warning when bucket usage crosses a threshold (default 80%). Configure it on the backend detail page.

docs.title: Third-party software
docs.text: IncubaCloud is built on software made by others, and each piece keeps its own licence. The full list, with each licence and how IncubaCloud uses it, is in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md in the core repository.

docs.title: In short
docs.text:
• Odoo Community (LGPL-3.0, Odoo S.A.) is the framework the panel runs on. The panel uses no Odoo Enterprise module.
  • Doodba (Apache-2.0, Tecnativa) is the base image of every instance the panel deploys and of the hosted service's panels, and doodba-copier-template (BSL-1.0, Tecnativa) is the template each instance's project is generated from.
  • queue_job (LGPL-3.0, Odoo Community Association) runs the panel's background jobs.
  • On your hosts, the panel installs Traefik, PostgreSQL, WAL-G, rclone, Grafana, Loki, VictoriaMetrics and other tools, as their authors publish them.

IncubaCloud's own code is licensed separately: see Licensing.

docs.title: Odoo Enterprise
docs.text: IncubaCloud deploys Odoo Community and Odoo Enterprise, but it does not provide Odoo Enterprise or a licence for it. To deploy Enterprise, you bring its code in your own repositories and you need your own Odoo Enterprise subscription ("On-premise") from Odoo S.A.

docs.text: Odoo is a trademark of Odoo S.A. IncubaCloud is not affiliated with Odoo S.A. Doodba is a name of Tecnativa, used here only to describe what IncubaCloud is based on.
